m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Gather the paper tools you'll use for the unplugged puzzles in this course.
  • Open the Scratch 3 editor on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook.
  • Check that it works by making the cat move with one click.
  • Decide, with a grown-up, whether to make a Scratch account.
  • Fix the problems that most often stop Scratch from loading.

A computer can add up a million numbers in under a second. Ask it to make you a sandwich, though, and it's stuck. It has no idea what "spread" means, which side of the bread is up, or when the sandwich is finished. Someone has to spell out every step, in the right order, with nothing left to guess.

That someone is a programmer, and spelling out steps is the skill this course teaches. You won't memorize a programming language here. You'll learn how to think about problems so that, whichever language you pick later, you already know what to tell it.

You need two kinds of tools: paper ones for thinking, and Scratch for testing whether your thinking works.

#Your paper toolkit

About half of this course happens away from the screen. Programmers do this too: they sketch a plan, walk through it by hand, and only then type it in. Collect these before Module 2:

  • A notebook (or a stack of paper in a folder). This becomes your algorithm notebook. The third lesson of this module shows how to lay out a page.
  • A pencil with an eraser. Pencil, not pen, because your first try at any algorithm will have a mistake in it. That's normal, and finding it is part of the work.
  • Grid paper, or plain paper with a grid you draw with a ruler. Module 3 has a robot that moves square by square.
  • A deck of playing cards, or ten scraps of paper numbered 1 to 10. Later modules use them for searching and sorting.
  • Sticky notes or small paper strips. Writing one step per strip lets you shuffle steps around until the order is right.
  • A helper (optional). A friend, sibling, or parent who will pretend to be a robot and follow your instructions exactly, even when that's silly.

None of this needs to be bought. Scrap paper and a pencil cover every activity.

#Your computer toolkit

  • A computer. A Windows laptop or desktop, a Mac, or a Chromebook. A tablet can build Scratch projects too, but dragging blocks with a finger is slow. A phone can only play projects, not build them.
  • A current web browser. Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari. Internet Explorer can't run Scratch 3.
  • An internet connection, or the free offline Scratch app (below).
  • A mouse (nice to have). Blocks are much easier to drag with a mouse than with a trackpad.

#Open the Scratch editor

Scratch is a free, block-based coding tool made at MIT. Instead of typing code, you snap colored blocks together, so you can test an idea in seconds without worrying about spelling or punctuation.

The quickest way in is the online editor. You don't need an account to use it.

Windows

  1. Open Chrome, Edge, or Firefox from the Start menu.
  2. Click the address bar at the top, type scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor, and press Enter.
  3. Wait a few seconds for the editor to load.
  4. Press Ctrl + D to bookmark the page so you can get back to it in one click.

Prefer an app that works offline? Go to scratch.mit.edu/download, choose Windows, and get the Scratch app from the Microsoft Store. Then open Scratch 3 from the Start menu.

macOS

  1. Open Safari or Chrome (both are fine).
  2. Click the address bar, type scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor, and press Return.
  3. Wait a few seconds for the editor to load.
  4. Press Cmd + D to bookmark it.

Prefer an app that works offline? Go to scratch.mit.edu/download, choose macOS, and either get it from the Mac App Store or download it directly. With the direct download, open the .dmg file and drag Scratch 3 into your Applications folder.

Chromebook

  1. Open Chrome.
  2. Click the address bar, type scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor, and press Enter.
  3. Wait a few seconds for the editor to load.
  4. Press Ctrl + D to bookmark it.

Prefer an app? Many Chromebooks can install Scratch from the Google Play Store; scratch.mit.edu/download links to it. School Chromebooks sometimes block Play Store apps, and that's fine: the browser editor does everything this course needs.

#What you should see

When the editor has loaded, you'll see three main areas:

If you see the cat, Scratch is working.

#A ten-second test

Find the blue Motion blocks on the left. Click once, right in the palette, on this block (you don't need to drag it anywhere):

The cat on the stage should shift a little to the right. Click it five more times and the cat keeps going. Clicking a block in the palette runs it once, which is a handy way to check what a block does before you use it in a script.

#Account or no account?

Both choices work for every lesson in this course.

No account With an account
Build and run projects Yes Yes
Where your work is saved A file on your computer, which you save yourself Online, in My Stuff, from any computer
Sharing projects with others No Yes, if you choose to
Needs a grown-up's help No Yes

To make one, click Join Scratch at the top of scratch.mit.edu. Scratch asks for a username, a password, your country, and your birth month and year. If you're young, it asks for a parent's or guardian's email address, and in some places a grown-up has to approve the account before it works. Do this together with that grown-up.

⚠️ Watch out

Keep your username anonymous. Scratch's own advice is "Don't use your real name." Leave out your school and your age too. "OrbitFox27" is a good username. "MayaLopez2014" tells strangers your name and roughly how old you are.

💡 Tip

Not sure yet? Start without an account. Everything you save as a file can be uploaded to an account later.

#When Scratch won't cooperate

  • The page stays blank, or says your browser isn't supported. Update your browser, or try a different one. On an old computer, Chrome or Firefox usually works best.
  • The site is blocked on a school computer. Ask your teacher whether scratch.mit.edu can be unblocked, or use a home computer. Every paper activity still works in the meantime.
  • Blocks won't drag on a tablet. Press and hold a block for a moment before you move your finger, or plug in a mouse.
  • Everything is slow. Close other tabs and apps. Scratch runs inside your browser, so a browser with 30 tabs open has less room for it.
  • The editor is in the wrong language. Click the globe icon at the top-left of the editor and pick your language.
  • There's no sound. Check your computer's volume and make sure the browser tab isn't muted. Sound is a small part of this course, so don't let it hold you up.

#Further reading

  • Download the Scratch app (opens in a new tab): the official install steps for each kind of computer, if you'd rather work offline.
  • Scratch for parents (opens in a new tab): a page written for grown-ups about what Scratch is and how accounts work. Good to read together.
  • Scratch FAQ (opens in a new tab): answers about accounts, privacy, and which devices Scratch supports.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a short list of plain-English steps into a Scratch script.
  • Predict what a script will do, then run it and compare.
  • See that a computer follows steps in exactly the order you give them.
  • Step through the same algorithm written in a text language.

Here are four steps. Read them and picture what happens before you build anything:

  1. Stand in the middle of the stage.
  2. Say "Watch me walk." for 2 seconds.
  3. Walk 150 steps to the right.
  4. Say "Made it!" for 2 seconds.

A list of steps that solves a problem is called an algorithm. You already follow algorithms all the time: a recipe, the directions to a friend's house, the rules printed inside a board game box. The difference in this course is who follows them. You'll write steps for a computer, which does exactly what you say and nothing you didn't say.

#Write your prediction first

Open your notebook and write one sentence: where will the cat be when the script finishes, and what will it have said, in what order?

This feels like a waste of time when the answer seems obvious. It isn't. A prediction is how you notice a surprise. If you don't decide what should happen, you can't tell when something goes wrong.

#Build the script, one block per step

Open the Scratch editor. Each block below matches one step of the algorithm, plus one block at the top that says when to start.

  1. Click the yellow Events circle. Drag when green flag clicked into the code area in the middle.
  2. Click Motion. Drag go to x: () y: () and snap it under the first block. You'll see a gray shadow where it will land; let go and it clicks into place. Click each number and change both to 0.
  3. Click the purple Looks circle. Drag say [Hello!] for (2) seconds under that. Click the word Hello! and type Watch me walk.
  4. Back in Motion, drag move (10) steps under that and change 10 to 150.
  5. From Looks, add another say block and change its text to Made it!

Your script should look like this:

Step 1 of the plain-English version, "stand in the middle", became go to x: (0) y: (0). The middle of the Scratch stage is the spot where x is 0 and y is 0. Module 3 explains these numbers properly; for now, think of them as the address of the center.

#Run it and compare

Click the green flag above the stage. Here is what happens:

Look at line 3 again. The algorithm said walk, but the cat didn't walk. It vanished from one spot and appeared at the next, because move changes the cat's position all at once. You meant "walk", you wrote "move 150", and the computer did exactly what you wrote. That gap between what you meant and what you said is the main thing this course will train you to spot.

Now check your work against this list. It's your proof that everything is set up:

  • The cat ends up to the right of the center.
  • The two bubbles appear in the right order, one after the other.
  • Click the flag again. The same thing happens, from the same starting spot.

If all three are true, your computer and Scratch are ready for the rest of the course.

#Order is part of the algorithm

🧪 Try it yourself

Pull the move (150) steps block out and snap it back in above the first say block. (Dragging a block also drags everything under it, so you may need to move the bottom blocks back afterwards.) Predict what will change, then click the flag.

Now the cat jumps right first and then says "Watch me walk.", which makes no sense: it has already gone. The blocks are the same five blocks. Only the order changed, and the program changed with it. Computers don't rearrange steps into the order you probably meant.

Try one more experiment. Right-click the go to x: (0) y: (0) block (on a Mac trackpad, Control-click) and choose Delete Block. Only that block disappears, and the blocks below it close the gap. Click the flag three times. The cat moves further right every time, until it bumps the edge of the stage.

The computer remembers where the cat is between runs. Without the go to block, each run starts from wherever the last one ended. That remembered information is called state, and Module 3 is all about keeping track of it. Put the go to block back (or press Ctrl + Z, Cmd + Z on a Mac, to undo the delete) before you continue.

#The same steps in a text language

Scratch is one way to write an algorithm. Most programmers type theirs in a text language such as Python. You don't need to learn Python for this course. These step-through animations let you watch a computer follow steps one line at a time, which is hard to see in Scratch because it runs so fast.

Press the step button and watch x, the cat's position, in the variables panel:

Notice that x stays at 0 while the first message prints. It only becomes 150 when line 3 runs. The computer does one step, finishes it, then moves to the next, in order, every time.

#If it doesn't work

⚠️ Watch out

Nothing happens when you click the flag. The top block must be the curved-top when green flag clicked from Events, and every block must be snapped on. If there's a gap between two blocks, the ones below the gap never run. Drag the lower block up until it clicks into place.

  • The script disappeared. Scripts belong to whichever sprite is selected. Look at the sprite list under the stage: the cat should be highlighted. If you had the stage (on the far right) selected, your blocks were added to the stage instead. Click the cat to find its scripts.
  • The cat moves the wrong way or the wrong distance. Check that 150 is in the move block, not in one of the go to boxes, and that there's no minus sign in front of it.
  • A bubble shows the wrong words. Click the white text inside the say block and retype it. Spelling inside the bubble doesn't break anything, but it's worth matching the plan.

Before you close the tab, keep this project. The next lesson shows how to save it, and how to find it again.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Save a Scratch project as a file and load it back.
  • Name and organize your project files so you can find them months later.
  • Set up an algorithm notebook page you can use for any problem.
  • Follow a five-step routine when you're stuck.
  • Know how the Notes, Build-along, and Practice lessons work.

Picture this: you spend 40 minutes getting a robot to drive around a room, you close the browser tab, and the robot is gone. Without a Scratch account, that's exactly what happens to work you haven't saved. The editor doesn't keep it for you. Two minutes of good habits now saves you from ever doing that work twice.

#Save a project to your computer

This works with or without an account, and in the Scratch app too.

  1. Click File in the menu bar at the top of the editor.
  2. Choose Save to your computer.
  3. Your browser downloads a file ending in .sb3. That one file holds everything: your sprites, scripts, sounds, and backdrops.

Some browsers ask you for a file name and a place to save it. Others save it straight to your Downloads folder with a name like Scratch Project.sb3. Here's where to find it:

Windows

Press Windows key + E to open File Explorer, then click Downloads on the left. Chrome and Edge also show recent downloads when you click the download arrow near the top-right of the browser.

macOS

Open Finder and press Option + Cmd + L to jump to your Downloads folder. In Safari, the download arrow in the top-right of the toolbar lists recent downloads.

Chromebook

Open the Files app from the launcher (or press Alt + Shift + M), then click Downloads under My files.

#Load it back

  1. Open the Scratch editor.
  2. Click File, then Load from your computer.
  3. Pick your .sb3 file.

⚠️ Watch out

Loading replaces whatever is in the editor right now. If you have unsaved work open, save it first, then load the other project.

#If you have an account

When you're signed in, the online editor saves to your account. Type a name for the project in the title box at the top of the editor, then use File › Save now before you close the tab. Your projects are listed in My Stuff, the folder icon in the menu bar.

Even with an account, save a copy to your computer now and then. A file on your own computer is a backup that doesn't depend on being online.

#Name files so you can find them later

By the end of the course you'll have a dozen or more projects. "Scratch Project (14).sb3" won't help you find the one you want. Make a folder called Computational Thinking in your Documents folder, and name every file the same way:

The module number goes first so the files sort in order. Next comes a few words about what the project does. When you're about to try something risky, save a -v2 copy first. If the experiment goes badly, the version that worked is still there.

#Set up your algorithm notebook

Your notebook is where you plan before you build and where you write down what really happened. Use this layout whenever a lesson gives you a problem:

Two habits make it far more useful. First, when a step turns out to be wrong, cross it out with one line instead of erasing it. Later you can see what you changed, which is exactly what you need when the same kind of bug shows up again. Second, always fill in Test before you look at the answer. Writing "I expected 3, I got 4" is the beginning of nearly every fix.

#How the lessons in this course work

Modules 2 to 7 each have three lessons:

  • Notes teach one big idea with everyday examples, diagrams, and a short video.
  • Build-along uses that idea to make one thing in Scratch, a step at a time. Each step adds a few blocks and tells you what you should see when you run them.
  • Practice gives you six problems that get harder as you go, then a challenge. Each has a folded hint and a folded solution. Give each problem at least five minutes of real effort before you open the hint.

Module 8 is a project of your own design.

Along the way you'll meet three special kinds of block in the lessons:

  • Quizzes. Pick an answer and you'll see why it's right or wrong. Every wrong option has an explanation, so a wrong pick still teaches you something.
  • Step-through animations. These show an algorithm written in Python, a text language. Use the step buttons to move forward and back one line at a time, and watch the variables change. You only need to read them, never write them.
  • Scratch blocks. They look like the real blocks in the editor, and the color tells you which category to find them in. Motion is blue, Looks is purple, Events is yellow, Control is orange.

#When you're stuck

Everyone gets stuck, including people who have programmed for years. The difference is that experienced programmers have a routine instead of staring at the screen hoping. Here's one:

  1. Say exactly what's wrong. "It doesn't work" can't be fixed. "The robot should stop at the desk, but it drives through the wall" can.
  2. Be the computer. Put your finger on the first step and do only what it says. On paper, track where everything is after each step. Usually the bug shows up as the moment where what the step says differs from what you meant.
  3. Shrink the problem. Pull a few blocks off and run just the first part. If that part works, add the next part back. You've cornered the bug when the program breaks right after you add a piece.
  4. Change one thing at a time. If you change three blocks at once and it starts working, you won't know which change fixed it.
  5. Ask for help, and bring your notes. Show your script, what you expected, what happened, and what you already tried. A good question often solves itself while you're writing it down.

Taking a five-minute break counts too. Coming back with fresh eyes finds bugs surprisingly often.

#Safety nets in Scratch

  • Undo. Right-click an empty part of the code area and choose Undo, or press Ctrl + Z (Cmd + Z on a Mac).
  • Restore. Deleted a whole sprite by accident? Edit › Restore Sprite brings it back.
  • Clean up Blocks. Right-click the code area and choose Clean up Blocks to line up scattered scripts neatly.
  • Add Comment. Right-click a block and choose Add Comment to stick a note on it, such as "this part resets the robot". Notes like that help the next person who reads your project, and that next person is usually you.

#Further reading

  • File Menu on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): exactly what each File option does, with and without an account.
  • Debugging Scripts on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): more ways to find bugs in Scratch projects, written by Scratchers.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe a problem by its goal, inputs, constraints, and output.
  • Break a big problem into smaller pieces you can solve one at a time.
  • Know when a piece is small enough to stop splitting.
  • Spot a piece that repeats, and solve it once.
  • Rewrite a fuzzy instruction so that anyone would follow it the same way.

Saturday, 9:55 a.m., at the Riverside Community Center. The coding club runs from 10:00 to 11:00. There are 6 working computers. There are 12 kids at the door, and more are walking up the path. The volunteer in charge, Ms. Okafor, got exactly one instruction from her manager: "Make it fair."

What should she actually do?

"Make it fair" is a wish, not a plan. Nobody can follow it step by step, because it doesn't say what to do first, or what "fair" means, or how anyone will know it worked. Turning a wish like that into steps is the first job of every programmer, and it's what this module is about.

#Start by asking what the problem actually is

Before solving anything, pin the problem down with four questions:

Question What it means At the community center
Goal What does "done" look like? Every kid gets the same amount of computer time during the hour.
Inputs What information do you start with? 12 kids, 6 computers, 60 minutes.
Constraints Which rules can't be broken? One kid per computer at a time. The club ends at 11:00. Nobody waits the whole hour.
Output What do you hand back at the end? A schedule: who uses a computer, and when.

Each row does a different job. The goal tells you when to stop. The inputs are the facts you'll work with, and they change: next Saturday there might be 9 kids, or 20. A good plan works for any inputs, not just today's. The constraints rule out answers that look fine but aren't allowed. "Give every kid the whole hour" is fair, but it needs 12 computers, and there are 6. The output is the thing you'll be able to point at and check.

Writing these down takes two minutes, and it catches a surprising number of mistakes before they happen.

#Decomposition: cut the problem into pieces

Nobody cleans a disaster of a bedroom by "cleaning the room". You do the clothes, then the books, then whatever is under the bed. Each of those is small enough to start right away.

Programmers call this decomposition: splitting a problem into smaller sub-problems, each simple enough to solve on its own, so that solving all of them solves the whole thing. If a piece is still too big, you split it again.

Here is Ms. Okafor's problem, decomposed:

Look at the bottom row. Every box is something Ms. Okafor could do right now, without asking anyone a question:

  • How many rounds? 12 kids ÷ 6 computers = 2 rounds.
  • How long is each round? 60 minutes ÷ 2 rounds = 30 minutes.
  • List kids in sign-in order. Use the sign-in sheet at the door.
  • Split the list into rounds. The first 6 names go in round 1, the next 6 in round 2.

That's the rule for when to stop splitting: stop when a piece is obvious. If you'd need to ask "but how?", it needs splitting again.

Decomposing also means you can check each piece by itself. If the schedule ends up wrong, you don't have to stare at the whole plan. You can check "how many rounds?" on its own, then "how long?", and find the piece with the mistake.

#Some pieces repeat, so solve them once

Look at "Run the turns". In round 1, she starts a 30-minute timer and the first 6 kids log on. When it rings, they log off. In round 2, she starts a 30-minute timer and the next 6 kids log on. When it rings, they log off.

That's the same piece twice. The only thing that changes is which kids are sitting down. So she can write it once:

...and then say "run one round, twice." If 18 kids show up, it's "three times", and the piece itself doesn't change at all.

Spotting a repeated piece is one of the most useful habits in programming. You solve it once, test it once, and reuse it. Notice the part that changes, though (here, which names). A reusable piece always has a blank in it that gets filled in differently each time. Module 4 shows how computers repeat a piece like this with loops.

#Turn each piece into instructions anyone can follow

Once you have pieces, each one needs instructions so clear that two different people would do the same thing. Here's the test: hand the instruction to two people. If they could do different things, it isn't precise yet.

Fuzzy Precise
Give everyone a turn. The first 6 names on the sign-in sheet use computers from 10:00 to 10:30.
Swap when it's time. At 10:30, those 6 kids log off, and the next 6 names log on until 11:00.
Be fair to latecomers. Anyone who arrives after 10:00 is added to the bottom of the list.

The fuzzy versions aren't wrong exactly; they just leave the important decisions to whoever happens to be reading. "Swap when it's time" could mean every 10 minutes, or whenever someone gets bored. The precise version can only mean one thing.

#Mistakes to watch for

⚠️ Watch out

A piece that's really the whole problem again. A plan with the step "make the schedule fair" hasn't decomposed anything; that's the original problem wearing a new label. Keep splitting until each piece is something you could do this minute.

⚠️ Watch out

Solving only today's numbers. "Split the kids into 2 rounds" works for 12 kids and 6 computers, and breaks when 18 kids turn up. Write the piece as a rule that uses the inputs: rounds = kids ÷ computers (rounded up when it doesn't come out even, which the next lesson handles). Then it works on any Saturday.

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting a constraint. It's easy to make a schedule that's fair and accidentally runs until 11:30. After you finish, read your plan against every constraint on your list, one at a time.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You're planning a class pizza order so that everyone gets 2 slices. Which of these is an input?

  • Right. It's a fact you start with, and it changes from class to class.

  • That's a rule the plan has to follow, so it's a constraint (or part of the goal), not an input.

  • That's what the plan produces at the end, so it's the output.

Show answer

A. Right. It's a fact you start with, and it changes from class to class.

2Which of these pieces still needs to be split further?

  • You could do this right now, so it's small enough.

  • You'd have to ask "but how?" That's the sign of a piece that's still too big.

  • This is a single, exact calculation. Nothing left to split.

Show answer

B. You'd have to ask "but how?" That's the sign of a piece that's still too big.

3Next Saturday, 18 kids come, with the same 6 computers and 60 minutes. Using the rules from this lesson, how long is each turn?

  • That's 60 ÷ 6, dividing by computers instead of rounds. Work out the rounds first.

  • 18 ÷ 6 = 3 rounds, and 60 ÷ 3 = 20 minutes each.

  • That's last Saturday's answer. A rule that only works for one set of numbers isn't a rule yet.

Show answer

B. 18 ÷ 6 = 3 rounds, and 60 ÷ 3 = 20 minutes each.

4Which instruction would two different volunteers carry out in exactly the same way?

  • "Done" means different things to different kids, so the swaps would happen at different times.

  • "Younger" and "a bit" both leave the details to whoever is reading.

  • Every part is exact: when, who, and what happens.

Show answer

C. Every part is exact: when, who, and what happens.

Key takeaways

  • Pin a problem down with four questions: goal, inputs, constraints, and output.
  • Decomposition splits a big problem into smaller pieces. Stop splitting when a piece is obvious.
  • Check each piece by itself; a mistake is much easier to find in a small piece.
  • When a piece repeats, solve it once and notice the blank that changes each time.
  • An instruction is precise when two different people would carry it out the same way.

#Further reading

  • Decomposition on BBC Bitesize (opens in a new tab): a short, clear explanation with everyday examples like brushing your teeth.
  • Introduction to computational thinking on BBC Bitesize (opens in a new tab): how decomposition fits together with patterns, abstraction, and algorithms, the other ideas in this course.

m2-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Plan a program as pieces on paper before building anything.
  • Use Scratch's ask block to collect inputs and variables to remember them.
  • Build and test one piece at a time, so every bug has a small place to hide.
  • Check a finished program against answers you worked out by hand.

Ms. Okafor from the community center doesn't want to do division at the door every Saturday. She wants a helper: type in the morning's numbers, and it tells her how many rounds to run and how long each turn is. You're going to build it in Scratch, and you're going to build it the way the last lesson described, one piece at a time.

#What we're building

When it's finished, a conversation with the helper looks like this:

Inside, it's four pieces, and you'll test each one before starting the next:

#Step 1: Plan it on paper

Open your notebook to a fresh page and fill it in before you touch Scratch:

Now work two examples by hand. These are your tests, so write the answers down.

  • 12 kids, 6 computers, 60 minutes: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 rounds, and 60 ÷ 2 = 30 minutes.
  • 9 kids, 6 computers, 60 minutes: 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5. You can't run one and a half rounds, so round up to 2. Each turn is 30 minutes, and 3 computers sit empty in round 2.

Why round up? If you round 1.5 down to 1, only 6 kids get a turn and 3 kids sit out the whole hour. That breaks the constraint "nobody waits the whole hour".

#Step 2: Make the variables

A variable is a labeled box where a program keeps a value it needs to remember. The helper needs five boxes.

  1. Click the orange Variables circle.
  2. Click Make a Variable, type kids, and click OK.
  3. Do the same for computers, minutes, rounds, and turn.

Each new variable appears in the palette with a checkbox beside it. Checked variables also show up on the stage as small boxes called monitors, which display the current value. Leave them checked; they're how you'll test each piece. (Scratch starts you with one called my variable. You can ignore it.)

#Step 3: Piece 1, ask for the inputs

The ask block and the answer block are in the light-blue Sensing category. The set block is in Variables; use its dropdown to choose which box to fill.

ask shows a question and waits until someone types a reply at the bottom of the stage and presses Enter. Whatever they typed goes into answer. The set block right after it copies answer into a variable, because the next ask will overwrite answer with a new reply.

Test it. Click the green flag and type 12, 6, and 60. Look at the monitors on the stage:

If a monitor shows the wrong number, the mistake is somewhere in these seven blocks and nowhere else. That's the reason for testing a piece before building the next one.

Notice something about this piece: it's the same two blocks, ask then set, three times. Only the question and the box change. That's the "repeated piece with a blank" idea from the Notes lesson, showing up in real code.

#Step 4: Piece 2, work out the rounds

This block has other blocks nested inside it. Build it from the outside in:

  1. Drag another set block from Variables under the last block, and choose rounds in its dropdown.
  2. From the green Operators category, drag (abs v) of () into the slot where the set block's number is. Click its dropdown and choose ceiling.
  3. Drag the () / () block into the slot of ceiling of.
  4. From Variables, drag kids into the left side of the division and computers into the right.

Ceiling rounds up to the next whole number: 1.5 becomes 2, 2.1 becomes 3, and 2 stays 2. It's exactly step 4 of the plan.

Test it with all three of these. Watch the rounds monitor each time:

⚠️ Watch out

Floor instead of ceiling. The same dropdown has floor, which rounds down. With floor, 9 kids gives 1 round, and 3 kids never get a computer. Scratch shows no error message, because nothing is broken as far as Scratch knows. The only way to catch this bug is to compare the monitor with the answer you worked out by hand in Step 1.

#Step 5: Piece 3, work out the turn length

Test it. 12, 6, 60 should give turn 30. Then try 18 kids, 6 computers, 60 minutes: that's 3 rounds, so turn should be 20.

#Step 6: Piece 4, announce the answer

The join block (in Operators) glues two pieces of text together, so the cat can say a number and a word in one bubble. To join three things, put a join inside another join.

Look closely at [ rounds.] and [ minutes.]. Each starts with a space. Without it, the cat says "2rounds." because join glues text together exactly as it is, adding nothing.

#The finished program

Save it as m2-fair-share-helper.sb3.

Here are the same steps in a text language. Each line of Python lines up with a piece of your script. input() is Python's version of the ask block, and int() turns the typed text into a whole number, which Scratch does for you automatically. Step through it and watch rounds and turn appear only once the earlier lines have run:

Python prints 30.0 where Scratch says 30. Both mean exactly thirty; Python just shows the decimal point after a division.

#Test it like you mean it

Run the finished helper with every row of this table, and compare what the cat says with the expected column:

Kids Computers Minutes Expected rounds Expected turn
12 6 60 2 30
9 6 60 2 30
6 6 60 1 60
18 6 60 3 20
7 6 45 2 22.5
0 6 60 ? ?

Predict the last row before you run it. With 0 kids, rounds is 0, and the helper then divides 60 by 0. Scratch's answer is Infinity, so the cat cheerfully announces "Each turn is Infinity minutes." Nothing crashed, but the answer is nonsense. Inputs like 0 that sit at the very edge of what makes sense are called edge cases, and Module 5 shows how to catch them before they reach the user.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the helper use ceiling rather than floor to work out the rounds?

  • Both take no noticeable time. The difference is the answer they give, not speed.

  • With 9 kids and 6 computers, floor gives 1 round, so 3 kids sit out the whole hour. Ceiling gives 2 rounds, so everyone gets a turn.

  • Scratch divides fine; 9 ÷ 6 gives 1.5. Ceiling only decides what to do with the .5.

Show answer

B. With 9 kids and 6 computers, floor gives 1 round, so 3 kids sit out the whole hour. Ceiling gives 2 rounds, so everyone gets a turn.

2Why did you test piece 1 before building piece 2?

  • Testing each piece as you go keeps the search for a bug small. Testing only at the end means a wrong answer could be coming from anywhere.

  • Scratch runs whatever blocks are snapped together. That's exactly what lets you test half a program.

  • Running a script doesn't save anything. Saving is File › Save to your computer.

Show answer

A. Testing each piece as you go keeps the search for a bug small. Testing only at the end means a wrong answer could be coming from anywhere.

3You type [rounds.] with no space at the start. What does the cat say for 12 kids and 6 computers?

  • That needs a space somewhere, and join never adds one by itself.

  • join sticks the two pieces together exactly as they are, with nothing in between.

  • Missing spaces never cause an error; the text just looks wrong.

Show answer

B. join sticks the two pieces together exactly as they are, with nothing in between.

Key takeaways

  • Plan the pieces on paper first, and work out test answers by hand before you build.
  • ask waits for typed input and puts it in answer; copy it into a variable straight away.
  • Build and test one piece at a time. A bug found right after you add a piece must be in that piece.
  • Some bugs make no error message at all. Comparing output with a hand-worked answer is how you catch them.
  • Unusual inputs like 0 can produce nonsense answers, even when the program runs without errors.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Make the cat also say how many computers sit empty in the last round. (That's an exercise in the next lesson.)
  • Some turns come out as 22.5 minutes. Use floor on the turn length so it always says a whole number of minutes.
  • Ask what time the club starts, and have the cat say when round 2 begins.

  • Variable on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how variables and their monitors work in Scratch.
  • Ask () and Wait on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): everything the ask block does, including what happens to answer.
  • The () of () block on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every option in that dropdown, including floor and ceiling, with examples.

What you'll learn

  • Name the goal, inputs, constraints, and output of a new problem.
  • Decompose a problem into pieces until every piece is obvious.
  • Find the repeated piece in a task, and the blank that changes each time.
  • Rewrite fuzzy instructions so they can only mean one thing.
  • Add a new piece to a Scratch program and test it on its own.

Work these in your notebook. Most are on paper; Exercise 6 uses Scratch. Every problem has more than one good answer, so if yours differs from the solution, check it against the problem's goal and constraints instead of the exact words.

Keep this process in view while you work. It's the whole module on one card:

#Warm-up: the sleepover

"Plan snacks for a sleepover. Five friends are coming, you have $20 to spend, and one friend can't eat nuts."

Which part is the goal? The inputs? The constraints? The output? Decide before you open the answer.

Show solution
  • Goal: everyone has snacks they can eat.
  • Inputs: 5 friends (6 people, counting you), $20.
  • Constraints: spend no more than $20; nothing with nuts.
  • Output: a shopping list.

The headcount is the easiest thing to get wrong. "Five friends" plus you is six people.

#Exercise 1: The class pizza order

A class of 26 students is having a pizza party. Each student gets 2 slices. Each pizza has 8 slices and costs $12. The class has $100.

Write the goal, inputs, constraints, and output. Then work out how many pizzas to order and whether the class can afford them.

Need a hint?

Decompose it: first work out how many slices you need, then how many pizzas that takes. If the pizzas don't come out to a whole number, think about which way to round. The fair-share helper had the same decision to make.

Show solution
  • Goal: every student gets 2 slices.
  • Inputs: 26 students, 2 slices each, 8 slices per pizza, $12 per pizza, $100 budget.
  • Constraint: total cost of $100 or less.
  • Output: the number of pizzas to order.

Round up for the same reason as the helper: 6 pizzas is only 48 slices, so two students would get one slice. With 7 pizzas there are 4 slices left over, and you can't make a fraction of a pizza appear.

#Exercise 2: Decompose your school morning

"Get ready for school" is one big task. Split it into 4 to 6 pieces. Then pick the piece that's least obvious and split it again, until every piece at the bottom is something you could do without thinking. Draw it as a tree, with the big task at the top.

Need a hint?

A good first split is by time (what happens first, next, last) or by place (bathroom, kitchen, bedroom, front door). "Get dressed" sounds simple, but could someone who had never seen your room do it?

Show solution

One good answer:

The detail that makes this work is in the bottom row. "Get dressed" became three pieces anyone could follow, and "leave" got an exact time. Your tree will look different; check that each bottom box passes the "could I do this right now?" test.

#Exercise 3: Thirty party invitations

Here's how someone wrote out making the first two invitations for a party with 30 guests:

Find the piece that repeats. What's the blank that changes each time? Which steps happen only once?

Need a hint?

Look for the lines that look the same except for a name. Then look at the first and last lines: do they happen once per guest or once in total?

Show solution

The repeated piece, written once:

The blank is the guest (their name and address). The whole plan becomes:

Thirty times four steps would be 120 lines written out. Now it's 3 lines plus a 4-step piece. Module 4 turns step 2 into a loop.

#Exercise 4: The pet sitter's note

A family going on vacation left this note for the neighbor's kid who is looking after their dog:

Rewrite it so that two different pet sitters would do exactly the same thing.

Need a hint?

Go word by word and ask "how much?", "when?", or "how would I know?" Words like some, if she needs it, a while, and too much are where two sitters would do different things.

Show solution

Every fuzzy word got replaced with an amount, a time, or a place. Notice that the rewrite also added information the sitter couldn't have guessed (where the food is). Precise instructions often need facts that only the writer knows.

#Exercise 5: Decompose a game before you build it

Here's a game idea: An apple falls from a random spot at the top of the screen. You move a bowl left and right with the arrow keys. Catching the apple scores a point, and a new apple falls. The game ends after 30 seconds and shows your score.

Don't build it. Decompose it: list the pieces the game needs, and mark which pieces repeat.

Need a hint?

Think about each thing in the game (the apple, the bowl, the score, the timer) and what it has to do. Then ask what happens over and over while the game is running.

Show solution

The repeated pieces are "fall down a little, again and again" and the whole apple cycle (start, fall, get caught or missed, restart). Splitting by thing works well for games, because in Scratch each thing usually becomes its own sprite with its own scripts.

#Exercise 6: Add a piece to the fair-share helper

Open m2-fair-share-helper.sb3. Add a new piece that makes the cat also say how many computers sit empty in the last round.

Work out the expected answer by hand for 12, 9, 7, and 18 kids (with 6 computers) before you build anything. Then test your new piece with all four.

Need a hint?

How many seats are there in total, across all the rounds? How many of those seats get used? Make a new variable called empty for the answer.

Show solution

Total seats across all rounds is computers × rounds. Every kid uses exactly one seat, so the unused seats are computers × rounds − kids. Every round except the last is full, so all of the unused seats are in the last round.

Add these two blocks at the bottom of the script, after the other say blocks.

If your answer for 7 kids is 1, you probably subtracted the wrong way around (kids − computers), which only happens to look right for some inputs. That's why the plan said to test four cases, not one.

#Challenge: The bake sale deadline

The class needs 120 cookies for a bake sale that opens at 3:00 p.m. Here's what you know:

  • Mixing the dough takes 30 minutes, and it has to be done before any baking starts.
  • You have 2 ovens. Each holds one tray of 12 cookies at a time.
  • A tray bakes for 15 minutes. Swapping trays takes no time.
  • The last trays need 10 minutes to cool before they can be sold.

What's the latest time you can start? Decompose the problem first, and write each piece's answer before combining them.

Need a hint?

Three pieces: the dough, the baking, the cooling. For the baking piece, work out how many trays you need, then how many rounds of baking two ovens take.

Show solution

The "rounds" piece is the fair-share helper in disguise: trays instead of kids, ovens instead of computers. Spotting that two problems share a piece is decomposition paying off twice. A careful planner would start earlier than 1:05, though. The plan has no room for a dropped tray, and real ovens need time to heat up.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain the three things that make a list of steps an algorithm: exact, ordered, and finishing.
  • Track state (where a robot is and which way it faces) as each step runs.
  • Name the inputs and outputs of an algorithm.
  • Use events to decide when an algorithm starts.
  • Find ambiguous steps by acting them out, and rewrite them.

A school office buys a small delivery robot to carry packages from the front door to the principal's desk. On its first day, someone types in: "Go to the desk." The robot rolls straight ahead, bumps into a table, and stops. It isn't broken. It did exactly what it was built to do with the instruction it got. The instruction just didn't say enough.

Robots, and computers in general, have no common sense to fill in the gaps. Every gap you leave, they fill with something literal, and usually wrong. This module is about writing instructions with no gaps.

#What makes a list of steps an algorithm

A recipe, a set of directions, and a Scratch script are all lists of steps. Here's what an algorithm has to have, stated exactly: it's a list of steps that is

  1. Exact. Each step means one thing. "Turn" isn't exact (which way? how far?). "Turn right 90 degrees" is.
  2. Ordered. It's always clear which step comes next.
  3. Finishing. It ends, and you can tell when. "Keep walking" never finishes. "Walk 4 squares" does.

"Go to the desk" fails the first test. It describes the goal, but it doesn't give the robot a single action it can do. The robot needs the steps that reach the goal.

#A robot on a grid

Here's the office as a grid. The robot only understands three commands:

  • F: move forward one square.
  • L: turn left 90 degrees, staying on the same square.
  • R: turn right 90 degrees, staying on the same square.

One algorithm that works: F F F F L F F F. The robot drives along the bottom row to column 5, turns to face up the page (north), and drives up three squares to the desk.

#State: what the robot "knows" after each step

To check that route, you have to keep track of two things after every command: where the robot is, and which way it's facing. Together, those are the robot's state. Every step either changes the state or leaves it alone.

After step Command Column Row Facing
start 1 1 east
1 F 2 1 east
2 F 3 1 east
3 F 4 1 east
4 F 5 1 east
5 L 5 1 north
6 F 5 2 north
7 F 5 3 north
8 F 5 4 north

Look at row 5 of the table. L changed the direction but not the position. Beginners very often move the robot a square when it turns, and then every step after that is off by one.

Here's the same route in a text language. Each line is one command, written as the change it makes to the state. Step through it and watch column, row, and facing in the variables panel:

The text after each # is a comment for human readers; the computer skips it. Notice the line for L only touches facing, just like the table.

#Inputs and outputs

Every algorithm takes something in and gives something back. A recipe takes ingredients and gives you a cake. Directions take a starting point and give you an arrival.

For the delivery robot:

  • Inputs: the map (where the tables are), the robot's starting square, the way it starts out facing, and where the desk is.
  • Output: the robot arriving at the desk.

Here's why that matters. F F F F L F F F only works if the robot starts at column 1, row 1, facing east. Turn the robot to face north before you start, and the very same commands drive it up the left side and straight into the wall. The starting state is an input, even though nobody typed it in. A precise algorithm either sets the starting state itself or says exactly what it has to be.

#Events: what starts the steps

Steps don't run by themselves. Something has to start them. In Scratch, that something is an event, and the yellow hat-shaped blocks in the Events category wait for one: the green flag being clicked, a key being pressed, a sprite being clicked.

Real life works the same way. "When the bell rings, line up." "When the microwave beeps, take the food out." The event is the when; the steps under it are the what.

These are two scripts on the same sprite, started by two different events. The green flag script sets the starting state: it puts the robot at the door and points it right (in Scratch, direction 90 means "facing right"). Each press of the space bar runs the second script once and moves the robot 50 steps. Press the space bar four times and the robot moves 200 steps, because each run starts from wherever the last one left it.

#Test for gaps by acting it out

You can't spot your own gaps by rereading, because your brain fills them in for you. You have to act it out: be the robot yourself, or ask a helper to follow your steps exactly, with no guessing allowed.

Try this instruction on the grid above: "Go forward until you reach the table, then turn and go to the desk."

Act it out. Facing east from column 1, row 1, the robot drives forward... and there is no table in row 1. It reaches the wall at column 5 and has no idea what to do. Even if it did reach a table, "turn" doesn't say left or right, and "go to the desk" is the goal again, not a step.

Words that almost always hide a gap:

  • Amounts without numbers: a bit, a few, for a while, enough.
  • Directions without a side: turn, go around, move over.
  • Stopping points the reader can't check: until it looks right, when it's ready.
  • "It" and "there", when there's more than one thing they could mean.

#Mistakes to watch for

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting the starting state. A script with no go to and no point in direction at the top starts from wherever the sprite was left last time. It might work the first time and fail the second, which is the most confusing kind of bug. Set the starting state at the top of every algorithm.

⚠️ Watch out

Mixing up the robot's left with yours. L means the robot's left. When the robot is facing down the page, toward you, its left is your right. If a route keeps going the wrong way after a turn, turn your notebook so the robot is facing away from you, and check again.

⚠️ Watch out

Counting the starting square. Going from column 1 to column 5 takes 4 moves, not 5. The robot is already standing on column 1. Count the gaps you cross, not the squares you see.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1On an empty grid, a robot starts at column 1, row 1, facing east. It runs F F L F. Where does it end up?

  • Two moves east take it to column 3, L turns it north without moving, and the last F moves it up to row 2.

  • That treats L as a move. Turning changes the direction only; the robot stays on its square.

  • That swaps columns and rows. Columns go across (east is +1 column), rows go up (north is +1 row).

Show answer

A. Two moves east take it to column 3, L turns it north without moving, and the last F moves it up to row 2.

2Which instruction would a robot find ambiguous?

  • Exact: one action, one amount.

  • Left or right? How far? And which door? A robot can't fill in any of that.

  • Exact: a direction and an amount.

Show answer

B. Left or right? How far? And which door? A robot can't fill in any of that.

3You click the green flag twice, and the robot ends up in a different place each time. What's the most likely cause?

  • move always moves exactly the number of steps you give it. Nothing here is random.

  • Without go to and point in direction at the top, the second run starts where the first one finished.

  • Clicking the flag restarts the script from the top. The problem is what the top of the script does.

Show answer

B. Without go to and point in direction at the top, the second run starts where the first one finished.

4For the algorithm "drive the robot to the desk", which of these is an input?

  • The same commands give different results from different starting states, so the start is something the algorithm depends on.

  • That's what the algorithm produces: the output.

  • The route doesn't depend on it at all, so it isn't an input to this algorithm.

Show answer

A. The same commands give different results from different starting states, so the start is something the algorithm depends on.

Key takeaways

  • An algorithm is exact, ordered, and finishes. A goal like "go to the desk" isn't an algorithm.
  • State is what's true right now: here, the robot's position and direction. Every step changes it or leaves it alone.
  • Turning changes direction, not position. Track both after every step.
  • The starting state is an input. Set it at the top of the algorithm.
  • Events decide when steps start. In Scratch, each hat block begins its own script.
  • Find gaps by acting your steps out literally, not by rereading them.

#Further reading

  • Algorithms on BBC Bitesize (opens in a new tab): a short guide to what an algorithm is, with examples from everyday life.
  • Kidbots from CS Unplugged (opens in a new tab): grid-robot activities you can play with a friend, one person as the programmer and one as the robot.

m3-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Plan a route as numbered steps and check it with a state table before building.
  • Use Scratch's x and y coordinates and directions to describe exactly where a sprite is.
  • Set a sprite's starting state with go to and point in direction.
  • Slow a program down with wait so you can watch each step happen.
  • Use a second event to reset the robot, and test from several starting states.

A delivery robot waits by the door of an office. Its job: carry a package to the laptop on the far side of the room, without driving through the pile of rocks someone has left in the middle of the floor. (It's a strange office.) You'll plan the route on paper, prove it works with a state table, and then make it run in Scratch.

#What we're building

Here's the stage seen from above, with the route the robot will drive. The numbers in brackets are positions on the stage, which Step 1 explains.

And here's the algorithm the robot will follow:

#Step 1: Learn the stage's addresses

Every spot on the Scratch stage has an address made of two numbers:

  • x says how far left or right. It runs from -240 at the left edge to 240 at the right edge.
  • y says how far up or down. It runs from -180 at the bottom to 180 at the top.
  • The center is x: 0, y: 0.

A sprite also has a direction, measured in degrees: 90 is facing right, 0 is facing up, -90 is facing left, and 180 is facing down. Position plus direction is the robot's whole state, just like column, row, and facing on the grid in the Notes lesson.

#Step 2: Plan the route and check it on paper

Write this plan in your notebook:

Now be the computer. Track the state after every step:

After step x y Direction
1 -180 -120 90 (right)
2 -60 -120 90 (right)
3 -60 -120 0 (up)
4 -60 80 0 (up)
5 -60 80 90 (right)
6 160 80 90 (right)

Moving right adds to x. Moving up adds to y. Turning changes only the direction. The final row puts the robot at (160, 80), right next to the laptop at (190, 80), and the route never comes within 100 steps of the rocks. The plan works before you've touched a single block. That's the value of checking on paper: a wrong number found here costs ten seconds to fix.

#Step 3: Set the stage

  1. Backdrop. Under the stage at the bottom-right, click the Choose a Backdrop button. Search for Xy-grid and click it. It draws the x and y axes on the stage, which makes positions easier to judge.
  2. Robot. Hover over the Choose a Sprite button (the cat face in the bottom-right corner of the sprite list), click the magnifying glass, search for Robot, and click it. You can delete the cat by clicking the small trash can on its thumbnail.
  3. Laptop and rocks. Add the Laptop sprite and the Rocks sprite the same way. Select each one and type its position into the x and y boxes above the sprite list: Laptop at x 190, y 80; Rocks at x 60, y -30.

Click the robot in the sprite list so that the code you build next belongs to it.

#Step 4: Set the starting state

set size to is in Looks; the others are in Motion. Click the green flag. The robot shrinks, jumps to the door, and faces right.

Test it. Drag the robot somewhere else on the stage, then click the flag again. It jumps back to the door. That's the whole point of these blocks: whatever state the robot was left in, every run starts from the same place.

#Step 5: The first leg, and why you can't see it

Add a move block for step 2 of the plan:

Click the flag. The robot appears at its new spot instantly. You never see it travel, because Scratch runs blocks far faster than your eyes can follow. Check that it worked by looking at the x box above the sprite list: it should say -60.

To watch the algorithm happen, slow it down. From Control, add wait (0.5) seconds after every move and every turn. The robot will still jump, but in visible steps, one per instruction.

#Step 6: The turns and the other two legs

Add steps 3 to 6 of the plan, each followed by a wait. In the Motion category, turn left is the block with the arrow curving counterclockwise (↺), and turn right has the arrow curving clockwise (↻).

Click the flag and watch. When the robot turns to face up, the whole picture tips sideways. That's Scratch rotating the sprite to show its direction, and it's handy here: you can see which way the robot is about to drive.

⚠️ Watch out

The robot heads down instead of up. You used turn right where the plan says turn left. The robot then drives toward the bottom of the stage, and because Scratch won't let a sprite leave the stage completely, it gets stuck at the bottom edge. Compare your blocks with the plan one line at a time; the arrows on the two turn blocks look very similar.

#Step 7: Deliver the package

Add the final step from Looks:

#Step 8: Add a reset button with a second event

It would be handy to put the robot back at the door without running the whole delivery. A second event can do that. Build this as a separate script, next to the first one:

Now pressing R resets the robot, and clicking the flag runs the delivery. Two events, two scripts, one robot.

#The finished program

Save it as m3-delivery-robot.sb3.

#Test it like a skeptic

A program that worked once hasn't been tested. Try to break it:

  1. Click the flag. Does the robot reach the laptop and say its line?
  2. Drag the robot to the top-right corner, and type 180 into the Direction box above the sprite list so it faces down. Click the flag. It should still deliver, because the script sets its own starting state.
  3. Click the red stop sign halfway through a delivery. Then click the flag. Does it start cleanly from the door?

🧪 Try it yourself

Press R while the robot is halfway through a delivery. The reset script puts it back at the door, but the delivery script doesn't stop: it carries on with its next blocks, starting from the door. The robot ends up somewhere strange. Two scripts were changing the same robot's state at once, and neither knew about the other. Keep that in mind whenever you give one sprite more than one event.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1After a full delivery, the robot is already facing right. Why keep point in direction (90) at the top of the script?

  • Someone could drag it, the stop sign could interrupt a run after a turn, or another script could turn it. Setting the direction makes every run start the same way.

  • Scripts can run without it. The block is there for reliability, not because Scratch demands it.

  • Direction has nothing to do with speed; it only decides which way move goes.

Show answer

A. Someone could drag it, the stop sign could interrupt a run after a turn, or another script could turn it. Setting the direction makes every run start the same way.

2What would you see if you removed all the wait blocks?

  • The moves and turns are the same, so the route is the same. Only the timing changes.

  • Scratch runs the moves faster than you can see. The waits don't change where the robot goes, only whether you can watch it get there.

  • Scripts don't need waits to run. They're for the humans watching.

Show answer

B. Scratch runs the moves faster than you can see. The waits don't change where the robot goes, only whether you can watch it get there.

3In step 3 you use turn right (90) degrees by mistake. What happens next?

  • Turning right from facing right points it down (180). Moving 200 steps from y -120 would take it far below the stage, so Scratch stops it at the bottom edge.

  • Scratch never guesses what you meant. It follows the block you used.

  • Turning around would need 180 degrees. A 90-degree right turn from facing right points it straight down.

Show answer

A. Turning right from facing right points it down (180). Moving 200 steps from y -120 would take it far below the stage, so Scratch stops it at the bottom edge.

Key takeaways

  • Check a plan on paper with a state table first. Wrong numbers are cheapest to fix before you build.
  • x is left and right, y is up and down, and direction 90 means facing right.
  • Set the starting state at the top of the script so every run starts the same way.
  • Computers run too fast to watch. A wait after each step lets you see the algorithm happen.
  • Each event starts its own script. Two scripts can change the same sprite at the same time, which can cause surprises.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Replace each move and wait pair with a glide (1) secs to x: () y: () block so the robot drives smoothly. What information do you need for each glide that you didn't need before?
  • Add a second stop: the robot delivers to the laptop, then goes on to another sprite somewhere else in the room.
  • Write a return trip that runs when you press the space bar. To drive the route backwards, you have to turn around, reverse the order of the legs, and swap every left turn for a right. Plan it on paper first.

#Further reading

  • Coordinate System on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how x and y positions work on the stage, with diagrams.
  • Direction on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): what the direction numbers mean and how rotation styles change the way a sprite turns.

What you'll learn

  • Put steps in an order that works, and spot which steps are allowed to swap.
  • Trace a grid robot's state by hand, and write a route around obstacles.
  • Name the inputs and outputs of everyday algorithms.
  • Find a missing starting state in a Scratch script.
  • Use events to control a sprite, and write instructions precise enough to draw from.

Grid exercises use the same robot as the Notes lesson: F moves forward one square, L turns left 90 degrees, and R turns right 90 degrees. Turning never moves the robot off its square. Columns are numbered left to right, and rows bottom to top.

#Warm-up: find the gaps

"Put a little sugar in the tea and stir it for a while."

Circle every word that two people might carry out differently.

Show solution

A little (how much?) and for a while (how long?). A precise version: "Put 1 teaspoon of sugar in the tea and stir it 10 times." It is fine here, because there's only one thing it could mean.

#Exercise 1: Breakfast, scrambled

These steps are out of order:

Write them in an order that works. Then answer: which steps could swap places without breaking anything, and which steps have to stay where they are?

Need a hint?

For each step, ask: "What has to have happened already for this step to be possible?" You can't pour into a bowl you haven't taken out.

Show solution

One order that works: B, D, A, E, C.

  • B must come first, because A and D need a bowl.
  • C must come last, because it needs the cereal, the milk, and the spoon.
  • E can go anywhere before C. Getting the spoon doesn't depend on the bowl at all.
  • A and D can swap, if you don't mind milk-first cereal.

Some steps depend on others, and those can't be swapped. Steps that don't depend on each other can go in either order. Algorithms often have more than one correct order for exactly this reason.

#Exercise 2: Be the robot

On an empty grid, the robot starts at column 1, row 1, facing north (up the page). It runs:

Where does it end up, and which way is it facing? Fill in a state table as you go.

Need a hint?

Facing north, F adds 1 to the row. After R, the robot faces east, so F adds 1 to the column instead. L and R never change the column or row.

Show solution
After Command Column Row Facing
start 1 1 north
1 F 1 2 north
2 F 1 3 north
3 R 1 3 east
4 F 2 3 east
5 F 3 3 east
6 L 3 3 north
7 F 3 4 north

It ends at column 3, row 4, facing north.

#Exercise 3: Write the route

The robot starts at column 1, row 1, facing north (^). Write the commands that get it to the desk D without driving through a table #.

Need a hint?

The robot can't go straight up: column 1, row 2 is a table. Look for a clear column that runs all the way from row 1 to row 5.

Show solution

Turn right to face east, drive 4 squares along row 1 to column 5, turn left to face north, and drive 4 squares up column 5 to the desk. Check it by tracing: every square the robot enters, (2,1) through (5,1) and then (5,2) through (5,5), is free.

Other routes work too, such as turning north at column 3, going east along row 2, and then north up column 5 (R F F L F R F F L F F F). That one takes 12 commands instead of 10. Module 7 is about comparing different correct answers like these.

#Exercise 4: Inputs and outputs

For each algorithm, name its inputs and its output:

  1. A vending machine selling a snack.
  2. A map app giving walking directions.
  3. A pancake recipe.
  4. A calculator adding two numbers.
Need a hint?

Inputs are what goes in before the algorithm can start (things you give it, or facts it needs). The output is what you get at the end.

Show solution
Algorithm Inputs Output
Vending machine Money, the button you press A snack, and maybe change
Map app Where you are, where you want to go, the map A list of turns to follow
Pancake recipe Flour, eggs, milk, a hot pan Pancakes
Calculator Two numbers Their sum

Notice that the map app needs the map itself as an input, even though you never type it in. Like the robot's starting state, some inputs are easy to forget because nobody hands them over.

#Exercise 5: It works once

This script is supposed to move the cat right, then up, then say "Here!". It works the first time you click the flag. The second time, the cat ends up somewhere else.

Explain what goes wrong on the second run, using a state table. Then fix it.

Need a hint?

A brand-new cat starts facing right (direction 90). Which way is it facing at the end of the first run? That's how it starts the second run.

Show solution

The first run starts facing right and ends facing up, because of the left turn. The second run begins from that state:

Second run x y Direction
go to -100 -100 0 (up, left over from run 1)
move 100 -100 0 0
turn left 90 -100 0 -90 (left)
move 100 -200 0 -90

The cat goes up and then left, ending at (-200, 0) instead of (0, 0). The script sets the starting position but not the starting direction. The fix is one block:

#Exercise 6: Remote-control robot

Save your delivery robot as m3-delivery-robot-v2.sb3, then add four scripts so the arrow keys drive the robot one step at a time. Here's the first:

Build the other three, then drive the robot to the laptop with the keys. Write down the keys you pressed, in order. Last question: in this version, who is following the algorithm?

Need a hint?

Each arrow needs its own when [ v] key pressed script with a different direction: up is 0, left is -90, and down is 180.

Show solution

The program no longer contains a route. Each event script is one tiny, exact command, and you are choosing the order. The list of keys you wrote down is the algorithm, and you were the one following it. Games work like this: the program handles events, and the player supplies the sequence.

#Challenge: Draw it blind

Sit back to back with a helper, each with grid paper and a pencil. Picture a simple house: a square for the walls, a triangle for the roof, and a door. Write instructions for drawing it without using the words "house", "roof", or "door". Your helper follows your instructions exactly, without looking at your paper and without asking questions. Then compare drawings, find each place they differ, and fix the instruction that caused it.

If you don't have a helper, write the instructions today and follow them yourself tomorrow, doing only what the words say.

Need a hint?

Give your helper a starting point they can find, like "the point where two grid lines cross, 3 squares up from the bottom edge and 3 in from the left edge." After that, describe every line with a direction and a length in squares.

Show solution

Steps 5 and 7 are where most first drafts go wrong. "Draw a triangle on top" leaves the size, the height, and which way it points up to the reader. Every line needs a starting point, a direction, and a length.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find the repeating unit in a list of steps, and the part that changes each time.
  • Replace repeated steps with a repeat loop.
  • Tell a counting loop from a condition-controlled loop, and pick the right one.
  • Decide which steps belong inside a loop and which belong outside it.
  • Spot a loop that will never stop.

The school office has to make 300 name labels for the science fair. Taped to the label printer is this:

Written out in full, that's 300 lines and 1,200 steps. Nobody reads 1,200 steps, and somebody would definitely skip line 147 by accident. Yet anyone can follow this one sentence: "For each name on the list: type it, print, peel, and stick." Spotting that pattern, and then writing it once, is what this module is about.

#Find the pattern first

Before you can shorten a list of steps, you need to see what's repeating. Look for two things:

  1. The repeating unit: the chunk of steps that happens again and again. For the labels, it's type, print, peel, stick.
  2. The part that changes: what's different each time through. For the labels, it's the name.

Sometimes nothing changes. Here are the moves that make a sprite trace a square:

The repeating unit is move 100, turn right 90, it happens 4 times, and nothing about it changes from one time to the next.

#A loop says "do this part again"

A loop is an instruction to run a group of steps more than once. Here's the square written the long way in Scratch, with eight blocks under the hat:

And here it is with the orange repeat block from Control. The blocks inside the repeat are the repeating unit:

Both scripts make the cat do exactly the same moves. The second one is shorter, but that's not the main reason to use it. Say you want each side to be 50 steps instead of 100. In the long version, you have to change four numbers and not miss one. In the loop version, you change one. Fewer copies means fewer places for a mistake to hide.

The blocks inside a loop are called its body. Each time the body runs is called a pass (or an iteration).

#Watch the part that changes

In the label job, the body is the same every pass, but the name it uses is different. Here's that loop in a text language. Step through it and watch name take a new value on every pass:

The body (the print line, indented under the loop) is written once and runs three times. The last line isn't indented, so it isn't part of the body: it runs once, after the loop has finished. Scratch shows the same thing by which blocks sit inside the repeat jaws and which sit below it.

#Counting loops and condition-controlled loops

There are two kinds of "do it again", and real life uses both:

  • Counting loops run a set number of times. You know the number before you start: 4 sides of a square, 300 labels, 20 jumping jacks. In Scratch, that's repeat (10).
  • Condition-controlled loops keep going until something becomes true. You don't know how many passes it will take: stir until the sugar dissolves, keep knocking until someone answers, print labels until the roll runs out. In Scratch, that's repeat until < >.

Here's a condition-controlled loop for the label printer:

Nobody counts the labels on a roll first. The loop checks the question, does one pass, then checks again, and it stops the moment the answer is yes.

And here's one in Scratch. The cat walks until it reaches the edge of the stage:

How many passes does that take? It depends on where the cat starts and how big it is, and the loop doesn't need to know. That's the giveaway: if you'd have to guess the number, use a condition.

Scratch also has forever, a loop that never stops on its own. Games use it to keep checking the keyboard for as long as the game runs. You'll stop a forever loop with the red stop sign.

#Inside the loop or outside it?

Every step in a looped task belongs in one of three places, and the rule is simple:

  • Before the loop: steps that happen once, to get ready. Turn on the printer.
  • Inside the loop: steps that happen once per pass. Type, print, peel, stick.
  • After the loop: steps that happen once, at the end. Turn off the printer.

Put a step in the wrong place and the program still runs; it just does the wrong thing. This script means to say "Done!" when the square is finished:

The cat says "Done!" four times, once after every side, because the say block is inside the jaws of the repeat. Drag it out and snap it under the loop, and it runs once, after the fourth pass.

#Mistakes to watch for

⚠️ Watch out

A condition that can never become true. This loop is meant to count down the labels left on a roll:

It adds 1 instead of taking 1 away, so labels left grows forever and never reaches 0. The loop never ends, and nothing after it ever runs. If a script seems frozen, look at the loop's condition and ask: does anything inside the body move it closer to being true? Click the red stop sign to end it, then change 1 to -1.

⚠️ Watch out

Off by one. A loop that draws a triangle needs repeat (3). A loop for 300 labels needs repeat (300). It's easy to type one more or one fewer, especially when counting fence posts versus the gaps between them. Check the count against a small example you can do by hand: does a 3-label version print 3?

The first and last quiz questions are about these two scripts.

Script A:

Script B:

Check your understanding

4 questions

1In Script A, what does the cat say, and how many times?

  • "Hooray!" is below the loop, not inside it, so it isn't part of the body.

  • The body is just the "Hip!" block, so it runs 3 times. The block after the loop runs once, when the loop is done.

  • That would be true without the loop. repeat (3) runs its body three times.

Show answer

B. The body is just the "Hip!" block, so it runs 3 times. The block after the loop runs once, when the loop is done.

2Which of these jobs needs a condition-controlled loop?

  • You know the count before you start, so a counting loop fits.

  • The number of students is known, so this is a counting loop (one pass per name).

  • You can't know in advance how many knocks it'll take. The loop stops when a condition becomes true.

Show answer

C. You can't know in advance how many knocks it'll take. The loop stops when a condition becomes true.

3In the label-printing loop, where does "Turn on the printer" belong?

  • It only needs to happen once, before any labels are printed.

  • Then the printer would get switched on 300 times, once for every label.

  • Then it would happen after all the printing, which is too late.

Show answer

A. It only needs to happen once, before any labels are printed.

4Script B freezes, and the cat never says "Made it!". Why?

  • They stop as soon as their condition becomes true. The trouble is this one's condition can't.

  • Moving 0 steps changes nothing, so every pass checks the same condition with the same answer. Nothing in the body moves it toward being true.

  • It can; the cat-walks-to-the-wall example in this lesson does exactly that.

Show answer

B. Moving 0 steps changes nothing, so every pass checks the same condition with the same answer. Nothing in the body moves it toward being true.

Key takeaways

  • To shorten repeated steps, find the repeating unit and the part that changes.
  • A loop writes the body once and runs it many times. Fewer copies means fewer places for mistakes.
  • Use a counting loop when you know the number of passes, and a condition-controlled loop when you don't.
  • Steps that happen once go before or after the loop; steps that happen every pass go inside.
  • A condition-controlled loop needs something in its body that moves it toward stopping.

#Further reading

  • Pattern recognition on BBC Bitesize (opens in a new tab): more examples of spotting what's the same and what's different between problems.
  • Repeat () on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how Scratch's counting loop works, with examples.
  • Repeat Until () on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): Scratch's condition-controlled loop, and how it checks its condition.
