m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Add the Pen extension so a sprite leaves a line wherever it moves.
  • Draw a square with repeated blocks, then replace them with a loop.
  • Turn a square into any regular shape by working out the turn angle.
  • Put a loop inside another loop to repeat a whole shape.
  • Use repeat until to stop on a condition instead of a count.

Loops are hard to see in most programs, because the computer repeats things so quickly. Drawing fixes that. Give the cat a pen, and every pass through a loop leaves a line on the stage, so you can count the passes with your eyes.

#What we're building

By the end, one click of the green flag draws twelve overlapping squares arranged in a ring, each one a different color, like the petals of a flower. Pressing S clears the stage and draws a square spiral that grows until it hits the edge.

The flower is a loop inside a loop. Here's its shape:

#Step 1: Add the Pen extension and set up

Start a new project (File › New). At the very bottom-left of the editor, under the block categories, click the Add Extension button. Choose Pen. A new dark-green Pen category appears at the bottom of the list.

The cat is big enough to hide the lines it draws, so shrink it, and build this setup script:

erase all wipes the previous drawing. pen down means "draw as you move" and pen up means "move without drawing".

Why pen up before go to? Because state carries over between runs. Say you stopped the last drawing halfway, so the cat is off to one side with its pen still down. Jumping to the center would draw a long stray line across your fresh, empty stage. Lifting the pen first, then moving, then putting it down is the drawing version of setting a robot's starting state.

Click the flag. Nothing visible happens yet, apart from the cat shrinking and moving to the center. That's correct: you've set the state, and nothing has moved with the pen down.

#Step 2: A square, the long way

Add four pairs of blocks under the setup:

Click the flag. The cat draws a square, going right, then down, then left, then up, and ends where it started, facing right again. Count the blocks you just added: eight, made of the same two blocks four times.

#Step 3: Spot the pattern and loop it

Delete those eight blocks (drag them back to the palette) and replace them with a repeat from Control, with one copy of the pair inside its jaws:

Click the flag. You get the same square from three blocks instead of eight. Now try changing 100 to 60. One edit resizes the whole square; in the long version you'd have needed four edits, all exactly right.

#Step 4: One number changes the shape

What if you want a triangle, or a hexagon? Here's the idea. By the time the cat has drawn the whole shape and is back where it started, facing the same way, it has turned all the way around exactly once. All the way around is 360 degrees. So each turn has to be:

turn = 360 ÷ number of sides

Shape Sides (repeat) Turn
Triangle 3 120
Square 4 90
Pentagon 5 72
Hexagon 6 60
Octagon 8 45
Almost a circle 36 10

Try three or four rows of the table, changing both numbers in your loop each time. For the 36-sided shape, shrink move to about 10 steps so it fits on the stage.

⚠️ Watch out

A triangle that won't close. If you remember that a triangle's corners are 60 degrees and use turn right (60) degrees, the cat draws three sides of a hexagon and stops with a gap. The cat turns by the angle outside each corner, not the angle inside it. Use 360 ÷ 3 = 120.

Put the loop back to a square (repeat (4), move (100) steps, turn right (90) degrees) before the next step.

#Step 5: A loop inside a loop

One square is one petal. A flower is twelve petals, each turned a little from the last. So repeat the whole square 12 times, turning 30 degrees after each one (12 × 30 = 360, all the way around again).

Drag a second repeat block so its jaws wrap around your square loop, and add a turn after the inner loop but still inside the outer one:

Click the flag and watch. The inner loop draws a square; the outer loop turns the cat and starts the next square.

How many times does move (100) steps run? The inner loop runs it 4 times, and the outer loop runs the inner loop 12 times, so it's 12 × 4 = 48 lines from just six blocks.

#Step 6: Color each petal

From the Pen category, add change pen (color v) by (8) inside the outer loop, just above the inner loop:

Because it's inside the outer loop but outside the inner one, the color changes once per petal, not once per side. Move it inside the inner loop and every side gets its own color instead. Try both and see the difference; where a block sits decides how often it runs.

#Step 7: A spiral that stops at the edge

Every loop so far has known its count in advance. This one won't. A square spiral draws a side, turns, and makes the next side a bit longer, over and over. How many sides fit before it reaches the edge of the stage? You could work it out, but you don't have to: let the loop check.

Make a variable called side (Variables › Make a Variable). Then build this second script next to the first:

The touching block is in Sensing; click its dropdown and choose edge. Press S. The spiral grows outward, and the moment the cat touches the edge, the loop stops and the cat speaks.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change change [side v] by (5) to change [side v] by (0) and press S. The cat traces the same tiny square forever, because nothing in the loop ever gets it closer to the edge. Click the red stop sign, then put the 5 back.

#The finished program

Save it as m4-square-flower.sb3.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You want a pentagon (5 sides). What should the turn be?

  • 360 ÷ 5 = 72. After five turns of 72, the cat has turned exactly once around and the shape closes.

  • That's the angle inside each corner of a pentagon. The cat turns by the outside angle, so 108 makes the lines cross into a star-like tangle that doesn't close after 5 sides.

  • Five turns of 60 is only 300 degrees, so the shape is left with a gap. 60 is the turn for a hexagon.

Show answer

A. 360 ÷ 5 = 72. After five turns of 72, the cat has turned exactly once around and the shape closes.

2In the flower, how many times does turn right (90) degrees run?

  • That's how many times the outer loop runs. Each outer pass runs the inner loop's 4 turns.

  • That adds the counts (12 + 4). Nested loops multiply: every outer pass runs the whole inner loop.

  • 12 outer passes × 4 inner passes = 48 turns of 90 degrees, plus 12 separate turns of 30.

Show answer

C. 12 outer passes × 4 inner passes = 48 turns of 90 degrees, plus 12 separate turns of 30.

3What goes wrong if you remove pen up from the start of the flower script?

  • The pen is still down from last time, so the go to jump draws a line from wherever the cat stopped. Lifting the pen first resets that piece of state.

  • Color comes from the pen color blocks. pen up only decides whether moving draws.

  • pen down comes later in the script, so the flower still draws.

Show answer

A. The pen is still down from last time, so the go to jump draws a line from wherever the cat stopped. Lifting the pen first resets that piece of state.

Key takeaways

  • Find the repeating unit, write it once inside repeat, and change one number instead of many.
  • For a regular shape, the turn is 360 ÷ the number of sides.
  • A loop inside a loop multiplies: 12 passes of a 4-pass loop runs the inner body 48 times.
  • Where a block sits (before, inside the inner loop, inside the outer loop, after) decides how often it runs.
  • Use repeat until when you can't easily know the count, and make sure the body moves toward the stopping condition.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Ask "How many sides?" and draw that shape using (360) / (answer) for the turn.
  • Make the flower from triangles or hexagons instead of squares. What does the outer loop's turn need to be for 18 petals?
  • Use the pen's stamp block to leave copies of the cat around the ring instead of drawing lines.

#Further reading

  • Pen Extension on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every Pen block, with what each one does.
  • Repeat () on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): more on counting loops, including loops inside loops.

What you'll learn

  • Find the repeating unit in a sequence, even when it doesn't divide evenly.
  • Rewrite long instructions as a loop, with each step in the right place.
  • Choose a counting loop or a condition-controlled loop for a job.
  • Predict how many times each block in a nested loop runs.
  • Build loops in Scratch that draw, count, and stop correctly.

Exercises 1 to 4 are on paper. Exercises 5 and 6 and the challenge use Scratch; start each one with File › New, and add the Pen extension for Exercise 5 and the challenge.

#Warm-up: find the unit

What's the repeating unit in each sequence, and how many times does it repeat?

Show solution

A is red, blue, blue, repeated 3 times.

B is 1, 2, 3, repeated 2 times, followed by an extra 1, 2. It doesn't fit evenly, and that's fine: a loop of 2 passes handles the repeating part, and two extra steps after the loop handle the leftover. Real tasks are often like this, with a pattern plus a few odd steps at one end.

#Exercise 1: Compress the dance

Here's a dance routine, written out in full:

Rewrite it as a loop. Then look inside your loop's body: is there a smaller pattern you could loop too?

Need a hint?

Find where the routine starts to repeat itself. Is the last move part of the pattern?

Show solution

The bow happens once, at the end, so it goes after the loop. Inside the body, clap, clap is a tiny pattern of its own:

Both versions are correct. For two claps, the first is easier to read. If the routine had ten claps in a row, the inner loop would be worth it.

#Exercise 2: Before, inside, or after?

The school office needs labels for 300 students. These are the steps, in no particular order:

Write the plan as a loop. Put each step before, inside, or after the loop, in the right order.

Need a hint?

For each step, ask: "Does this happen once per student, or once for the whole job?"

Show solution

The four steps inside the loop happen 300 times each; the other four happen once. Steps 7 and 8 could swap without causing a problem. Did you notice a hidden question, too? One label roll probably doesn't hold 300 labels. A real plan needs a check inside the loop for an empty roll, and Module 5 is about adding decisions like that.

#Exercise 3: Counting or condition?

For each job, decide whether you'd use a counting loop or a condition-controlled loop, and say why in a few words.

Need a hint?

Before the job starts, could you write down exactly how many passes it'll take? If yes, it's a counting loop.

Show solution
Job Loop Why
a Counting 8 plants, known in advance
b Condition You stop when the water reaches the line, however long it takes
c Condition It might take 1 shuffle or 20
d Counting, twice A loop of 3 sets, each with a loop of 10: a nested counting loop
e Condition You don't know which page the chapter starts on
f Counting One pass per name, and the list says how many

#Exercise 4: Predict the nested loop

Don't run this yet. Predict how many times the cat says each word, and how long the whole script takes.

Then build it and check, using a clock or by counting out loud.

Need a hint?

Make a table with one row per pass of the outer loop, and write down every word said in that pass. Then add up the times.

Show solution
  • Ready: 2 times (once per outer pass).
  • Go!: 6 times (3 per outer pass × 2 passes).
  • Finished: once, after both loops.

Time: each outer pass takes 1 + 3 × 0.5 = 2.5 seconds, so two passes take 5 seconds. Add 1 second for "Finished": 6 seconds in total.

#Exercise 5: Draw a staircase

Use the Pen extension to draw a staircase of 5 steps going up and to the right. Each step is 30 steps wide and 30 steps tall. Start the pen at x -150, y -150, facing right. The cat should finish at the center of the stage.

Need a hint?

Find the repeating unit by drawing one stair with your finger: along, up, and back to facing along. That needs two moves and two turns. Remember to set the starting state with the pen up.

Show solution

Each pass moves the cat 30 to the right and 30 up, so after 5 passes it's at x -150 + 150 = 0 and y -150 + 150 = 0, the center. The turn right at the end of the body puts the cat back to facing right, ready for the next stair. Leave it out, and the second pass heads off to the left.

#Exercise 6: The rocket countdown

Make the cat count down from 10 to 1, saying each number for 1 second, then say "Liftoff!". Use a variable called count and a repeat until loop.

Once it works, answer this: what does the cat say if you swap the two blocks inside your loop?

Need a hint?

Set count to 10 before the loop. Inside the body, say the number, then make it one smaller. When should the loop stop?

Show solution

Trace the last two passes. With count at 1, the loop checks "is it 0?", gets no, says 1, and changes count to 0. On the next check the answer is yes, so the loop stops before saying 0.

If you swap the two blocks, the number goes down before it's said, so the cat says 9, 8, ..., 1, 0, and never says 10. Same blocks, different order, off by one at both ends.

A repeat (10) loop would also work here, since you know the count in advance. repeat until is a better fit for the way people describe a countdown: keep going until you reach zero.

#Challenge: The any-shape machine

Make the cat ask "How many sides?" and then draw a regular shape with that many sides. The shape should stay about the same size whatever number you type, so the total length of all the sides should always be 300 steps.

Test it with 3, 4, 6, and 40. Then try 2 and 1, and explain what you see.

Need a hint?

The answer to the question can go straight into a repeat block. You need two calculations: the length of each side (300 shared among the sides) and the turn (360 shared among the corners). Both are divisions using answer.

Show solution

With 40 sides, each side is 7.5 steps and each turn is 9 degrees, which looks like a circle. With 2, the cat moves 150 steps, turns 180 degrees, and comes straight back: a "shape" with two sides is a line drawn twice. With 1, it heads right for 300 steps (the edge of the stage stops it before then) and turns all the way around to face the same way: just a line. The program follows its rule correctly; the inputs are what don't make sense as shapes. Inputs like these are edge cases, and Module 5 is about handling them on purpose.

#Watch a loop inside a loop run

If Exercise 4 or the staircase felt slippery, this helps. A theater has 2 rows with 3 seats each, and this program prints a ticket for every seat. Step through it and watch row and seat. The inner loop runs all of its passes for every single pass of the outer loop, so seat goes 1, 2, 3 while row stays at 1, and only then does row become 2.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a rule as a condition that is either true or false.
  • Use if/else so a program takes exactly one of two paths.
  • Combine conditions with and, or, and not, and predict the result.
  • Put several decisions in a sensible order as a decision tree.
  • Find edge cases by testing a boundary, one value below it, and one above it.

The library on Maple Street has a self-checkout kiosk with one simple rule: nobody may have more than 5 books out at once. Jada already has 5. She scans a sixth, and the screen says Enjoy your book!

The kiosk did exactly what it was told. Its programmer wrote the rule as "refuse if books out is more than 5," and 5 is not more than 5. So Jada walked out with 6 books. Nothing crashed, and no error appeared. The rule was one number off, and only someone standing exactly at the limit could ever notice.

Programs make decisions like this all day, from logging you in to charging for shipping. This module is about writing them precisely and hunting down the cases, like Jada's, that slip through.

#A condition is a question with only two answers

A condition is a yes-or-no question a computer can check right now. "Is it raining?" works. "What's the weather like?" doesn't, because its answer isn't yes or no. Programmers say true and false instead of yes and no, and call a true-or-false value a Boolean, after the mathematician George Boole.

In Scratch, conditions are the pointy-ended hexagon blocks, and they only fit into pointy slots. The three comparison blocks live in the green Operators category:

Here is what the first two say for a few different values:

Condition value is 3 value is 5 value is 7
books out < 5 true false false
fines > 5 false false true

Look at the middle column. When the value is exactly 5, both comparisons are false: 5 isn't less than 5, and it isn't more than 5 either. Remember that column. It's where most decision bugs live.

📝 Note

Scratch's = block ignores capital letters, so YES, Yes, and yes all count as equal to yes. Most text languages are stricter. In Python, "YES" == "yes" is false.

#if/else: two roads, and exactly one gets taken

An if/else decision checks a condition once, then takes one of two paths. Here is the kiosk's rule as plain-English steps:

  1. Ask how many books the person has out.
  2. If that number is less than 5, say "You can borrow it."
  3. Otherwise, say "Please return a book first."

Here is the same algorithm as a flowchart. The diamond is the decision, and every diamond has exactly two arrows leaving it: one for true, one for false.

In Scratch it becomes the if <> then … else block from the orange Control category:

Try it with 4, then 5, then 6. Whatever you type, exactly one say block runs: never both, never neither. That guarantee is what else is for. A plain if with no else is different: when its condition is false, it skips everything inside and does nothing. That's fine for optional extras ("if it's your birthday, play a song") but wrong when everyone who walks up needs an answer.

#Combining conditions with and, or, not

Real rules come in bundles. The Maple Street kiosk actually checks several things: the card is active, the person has fewer than 5 books out, and they owe less than $5 in fines. Scratch has three blocks for gluing conditions together:

  • and is true only when both sides are true. "You can borrow if you have room and you owe less than $5."
  • or is true when at least one side is true. "Free entry for kids under 5 or people 65 and up." Ages here are whole numbers, so "over 64" means 65 and up.
  • not flips true to false and false to true.

A truth table lists every combination, so nothing is left to guesswork:

A B A and B A or B
true true true true
true false false true
false true false true
false false false false

and is the strict one: it says true in only one row out of four. or is the generous one: it says false in only one row.

⚠️ Watch out

Using or when the rule needs and. Someone writes the borrowing rule as <<(books out) < (5)> or <(fines) < (5)>>. Now a person with 2 books out and $40 in fines can borrow, because one true side is enough for or. When a rule says "both of these must be true," you need and. Read the condition out loud with one specific person in mind ("2 books, owes $40…") and check that the answer matches the library's policy.

#Decision trees: asking questions in the right order

One giant and can tell a person yes or no, but not why. A good kiosk says "your card has expired" or "you owe $7.50," so the person knows what to fix. To do that, ask the questions one at a time and give each "no" its own message. Drawn out, that's a decision tree:

The order matters. The card check goes first because without a valid card, the kiosk can't look up anyone's books or fines. Ask the questions that make the others pointless first.

Here is the same tree in a text language, Python. You don't need to know Python: read return as "give this answer and stop," and >= as "is at least." Step through it and watch which lines get skipped. As soon as a check fails, the later questions are never asked.

The second call is Jada. The rule now says books_out >= 5, so it refuses at 5 or more, which is what the library meant all along.

#Edge cases: the inputs at the corners

An edge case is an input sitting right on the boundary of a rule, or an unusual input the programmer never pictured. Jada's 5 books were an edge case. So is a fine of exactly $5.00, a person with 0 books out, a blank answer, or someone who types "five" instead of 5.

Here's a method that finds most of them. For every number in a rule, test the number itself, one value just below it, and one just above it. Then add the strange inputs.

Test Books out Fines Expected Why this test
1 4 0 borrow just under the limit
2 5 0 refuse exactly on the limit
3 6 0 refuse over the limit (shouldn't happen, but might)
4 2 4.99 borrow just under the fine limit
5 2 5.00 refuse exactly on the fine limit
6 0 0 borrow the smallest sensible value
7 -1 0 ??? an impossible value

Test 7 is the interesting one. The library's rules never say what to do with a negative number. Spotting gaps like that is part of a programmer's job: you take the question back to whoever wrote the rules (here, the librarian) and decide together.

⚠️ Watch out

Two separate if blocks that leave a gap. This looks like it covers everyone:

Type 5 and the kiosk says nothing at all, because both conditions are false at exactly 5 (the middle column again). Use one if <> then … else block instead, so every input lands on exactly one path.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The kiosk uses <(books out) < (5)> to decide who can borrow. Jada has exactly 5 books out. What happens?

  • That needs the condition to be true, but 5 is not less than 5.

  • At exactly 5 the condition is false, so the else path runs. That matches the library's real rule: 5 books is the maximum.

  • An if/else always runs one of its two paths, so the kiosk always says something.

Show answer

B. At exactly 5 the condition is false, so the else path runs. That matches the library's real rule: 5 books is the maximum.

2A water park lets you on the big slide if you are at least 120 cm tall and at least 10 years old. Who gets on?

  • He passes the height check but not the age check, and and needs both.

  • She's exactly on both limits, and "at least" includes the limit itself, so both checks are true.

  • Old enough, but not tall enough. With and, one false side makes the whole condition false.

Show answer

B. She's exactly on both limits, and "at least" includes the limit itself, so both checks are true.

3You're testing the rule "fines under $5 are OK." Which set of test values tells you the most?

  • All three are far below the limit, so they'd pass even if the boundary were wrong.

  • All far above it. A rule that's off by a little near $5 would still get these right.

  • These sit right on both sides of the boundary, which is exactly where a wrong < or > shows up.

Show answer

C. These sit right on both sides of the boundary, which is exactly where a wrong < or > shows up.

Key takeaways

  • A condition is a true-or-false question. In Scratch it's a hexagon block.
  • if <> then … else always runs exactly one of its two paths; a plain if may run nothing.
  • and needs both sides true, or needs at least one, and not flips the answer.
  • A decision tree asks one question at a time so every "no" can explain itself. Put the questions that make the rest pointless first.
  • Test every boundary three ways: just below, exactly on, and just above. Then try the weird inputs.

#Further reading

  • If () Then, Else (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): how the block runs, with example scripts you can copy.
  • Boolean Block (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): a list of every hexagon block in Scratch and what each one checks.
  • () = () (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): the surprising ways Scratch compares text and numbers, including why capitals don't matter.

What you'll learn

  • Save typed replies in variables with ask and set.
  • Turn each library rule into its own check with a clear message.
  • Use or to accept more than one spelling, and not to say "5 or more."
  • Write a test table before testing, then use it to find and fix a real bug.

#What we're building

The Maple Street library wants its kiosk rebuilt, and this time it has to explain itself. Here is a full conversation with the finished version:

These are the head librarian's rules:

  1. Your card must be active.
  2. Reference books, like encyclopedias, never leave the building.
  3. You may have at most 5 books out, so you can borrow only if you have 4 or fewer right now.
  4. If you owe $5 or more in fines, pay them before borrowing.

The script checks them in that order. Each check either lets the person through to the next one or explains the problem and stops:

You'll build one rule at a time and test each one as you go. At the end, a test table will catch a bug that none of the four rules mention.

#Step 1: Set up the project and ask the first question

  1. Go to scratch.mit.edu (opens in a new tab) and click Create.
  2. The cat can be the kiosk, or hover over the Choose a Sprite button (bottom right of the sprite list) and pick something else.
  3. Click the orange Variables category, then Make a Variable. Make four variables, each For all sprites: card, reference, books out, and fines.

Now build this first script on the kiosk sprite:

Click the green flag and type yes. The card monitor on the stage now shows yes.

Why copy answer into card? The light-blue answer block only remembers the most recent reply. By the end of this script you'll have asked four questions, and the first reply would be long gone. Copying each reply into its own variable keeps all four.

#Step 2: The card rule, with an early exit

Snap this under the set block:

stop [this script v] (in Control) ends the script on the spot. So a person with an inactive card never gets asked about fines, just like the decision tree in the Notes. Explain the problem, then stop.

Test it three ways. yes gives "Card OK." no sends you to the front desk. YES also works, because Scratch's = ignores capitals.

Now type y. The kiosk sends you to the front desk! Lots of people type y for yes, and the rule as written refuses them. Drag the = block out of the if, drop in an or block, and put one = block on each side:

Run it with y again. Card OK.

#Step 3: Reference books stay in the building

Add the second question and its check:

There's no else this time. If the book isn't a reference book, there's nothing to say yet, so the script simply moves on to the next question. A plain if is the right block whenever one of the two paths is "do nothing."

#Step 4: The books-out limit

Why > 4 and not > 5? The rule means "5 at most after borrowing," so someone who already has 5 must be refused. > 4 refuses 5, 6, 7, and up, and lets 0 through 4 pass. That's Jada's bug from the Notes, fixed before it ever ships.

Test with 4 (you move on to the next question) and 5 (refused).

#Step 5: Fines, and saying "5 or more" without a ≥ block

The rule says $5 or more blocks borrowing. Scratch has <, >, and =, but no "greater than or equal to" block. You could write <<(fines) > (5)> or <(fines) = (5)>>, but there's a neater way: "5 or more" means the same as "not less than 5."

Read the condition out loud: "if not fines-less-than-5." With $4.99, fines < 5 is true, not flips it to false, and the person passes. With exactly $5, fines < 5 is false, not makes it true, and the kiosk refuses.

Why not reuse the > 4 trick from Step 4? Because money has cents. A person owing $4.50 is under the limit, but 4.50 > 4 is true, so they'd be wrongly refused. The > 4 trick only works for things you can't have half of, like books.

#Step 6: Write the test table, then run it

Before clicking anything else, write down what should happen. A test table has one row per test, and the Expected column gets filled in before you run a single test, so the program can't talk you into its answer.

# Card Reference Books out Fines Expected
1 yes no 0 0 Enjoy your book
2 Y no 4 4.99 Enjoy your book
3 yes no 5 0 Return one first
4 yes no 2 5 Pay fines first
5 no See the front desk
6 yes yes Stays in the library
7 yes no -3 0 That number can't be right
8 yes no 2 -10 That number can't be right

Tests 7 and 8 come from a question you took back to the librarian: "what should happen with a negative number?" Her answer: someone typing -3 has made a typo, so tell them and let them try again.

Now run all 8 in Scratch and write down what actually happens. Clicking the green flag eight times and typing four answers each time gets tedious, so here is the same kiosk in Python, a text language, running all 8 tests in a row. You don't need to read every line. .lower() turns text into lowercase first, which copies what Scratch's = does for free. Look at the output.

Tests 1 to 6 pass. Tests 7 and 8 fail: the kiosk happily lends a book to someone with -3 books out, because nothing in the script ever asked whether the number made sense. Your Scratch kiosk does exactly the same thing.

#Step 7: Fix the bug, then re-run every test

Add a sanity check right after each number comes in. This one goes straight after set [books out v] to (answer):

Put a matching check after set [fines v] to (answer), using (fines) instead. Then run all eight tests again, not just 7 and 8. A fix in one place can break something that used to work, and the only way to know it didn't is to check.

Here is the Python kiosk with the same two checks added, re-running the whole table:

All eight pass.

#The finished kiosk

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the kiosk copy answer into books out instead of just using answer in the later checks?

  • answer holds whatever was typed, numbers included.

  • After the fines question, answer holds the fines, so the books-out reply would be lost. A variable keeps each reply safe.

  • Speed isn't the issue here; keeping each reply is.

Show answer

B. After the fines question, answer holds the fines, so the books-out reply would be lost. A variable keeps each reply safe.

2The books rule uses <(books out) > (4)>, but the fines rule uses <not <(fines) < (5)>>. Why not use > 4 for fines too?

  • not works with any condition at all.

  • 4.50 > 4 is true. The > 4 shortcut only works for whole numbers, like a count of books.

  • 5 > 4 is true, so they'd be refused, which is correct. The problem is with amounts between 4 and 5.

Show answer

B. 4.50 > 4 is true. The > 4 shortcut only works for whole numbers, like a count of books.

3A friend suggests replacing the four checks with one big and block that only says "yes" or "no." What would the kiosk lose?

  • The yes/no answers could match, but something people need would disappear.

  • With one combined condition there's only one "no" message, so nobody would know whether to renew a card, return a book, or pay a fine.

  • Not if the combined condition is correct. The loss is the explanation, not the decision.

Show answer

B. With one combined condition there's only one "no" message, so nobody would know whether to renew a card, return a book, or pay a fine.

Key takeaways

  • Copy answer into a variable right away whenever a script asks more than one question.
  • A run of separate checks that each explain the problem and stop keeps a decision tree flat and easy to read.
  • or lets one rule accept several spellings; not <() < (5)> is how Scratch says "5 or more."
  • Fill in the Expected column before you test, and re-run every test after every fix.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Kids' cards: readers under 13 may have only 3 books out. Ask for an age, set a limit variable to 3 or 5 with if/else, then compare books out to (limit) - (1).
  • Accept more replies: let n and nope count as no, and make the kiosk say "Please answer yes or no" for anything else.
  • Count checkouts: add a checkouts today variable that goes up by 1 after each successful loan. Think about where to reset it (hint: not under the green flag).

#Further reading

  • Ask () and Wait (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): how ask and answer work together, with example scripts.
  • Stop () (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): the difference between stopping this script, other scripts, and everything.
  • Not () (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): more everyday uses for not, like checking that a variable is not a certain value.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a written rule into the right mix of if/else, and, or, and not.
  • Choose test values that sit on and around every boundary.
  • Spot and fix overlapping conditions and rules that use the wrong operator.
  • Order nested decisions so the most specific rule is checked first.

Each exercise gives you a rule and asks you to build or fix a decision in Scratch. Write the plain-English steps on paper first, then build the script, then test it with values on both sides of every boundary. Try each one properly before you open the solution.

#Warm-up: true or false?

Say x is 7 and y is 10. Is each condition true or false?

Show solution
  1. false: 7 is not more than 10.
  2. true.
  3. false: the left side is true, but 10 < 10 is false, and and needs both.
  4. true: the left side is false, but y = 10 is true, and or needs only one.
  5. false: 7 < 10 is true, and not flips it.

#Exercise 1: Movie ticket prices

A cinema charges $6 for kids under 12, $7 for people 65 and older, and $10 for everyone else. Build a script that asks for an age and says the price. Then test it with 11, 12, 30, 64, and 65.

Need a hint?

Three possible prices means two decisions. Put the second if/else inside the else of the first one. And since ages are whole numbers, "65 and older" can be written as > 64.

Show solution

The tests: 11 → $6, 12 → $10, 30 → $10, 64 → $10, 65 → $7. Ages 12 and 65 are the edges, and they're exactly the ones a wrong < or > would get wrong. Each age lands on exactly one say, because every path through nested if/else blocks ends in exactly one place.

#Exercise 2: Fix the roller coaster

The sign says: riders must be at least 120 cm tall and at least 8 years old. Someone built this:

There are two different bugs. For each one, find a rider (a height and an age) who gets the wrong answer, then fix the script.

Need a hint?

Picture a rider who is tall but young, and run them through the condition. Then picture a rider who is exactly 120 cm and exactly 8.

Show solution

Bug 1: or should be and. A rider who is 150 cm tall but only 5 years old gets "Enjoy the ride!", because one true side is enough for or. The sign says both must be true.

Bug 2: > leaves out the limit. A rider who is exactly 120 cm and exactly 8 is refused, because 120 > 120 is false. "At least" includes the limit.

The fix uses "not less than" for both checks, which is how Scratch says "at least" and also works for heights like 119.5 cm:

#Exercise 3: Why does everyone get a C?

This script is supposed to turn a test score into a letter grade: 90 and up is an A, 80 to 89 is a B, 70 to 79 is a C.

Before you run it, predict what the sprite ends up saying for a score of 95. Then explain why, and fix it.

Need a hint?

Walk through the script with 95, one block at a time. How many of the three conditions are true? A say block with no time replaces whatever the sprite was saying a moment ago.

Show solution

It ends up saying C. For 95, all three conditions are true, so all three say blocks run, one right after the other. Each one replaces the last, and C comes last. The conditions overlap: every score above 89 is also above 79 and above 69.

The fix is a chain of if/else blocks, so that once one grade matches, the rest are skipped:

Test 90, 89, 80, 79, 70, and 69: each pair sits on either side of a boundary.

#Exercise 4: A rock-paper-scissors judge

Two players type their moves into variables you and friend (each one is rock, paper, or scissors). Build a script that says who wins or that it's a tie. Before you build it, work out how many different games are possible and draw the decision on paper.

Need a hint?

There are 3 × 3 = 9 possible games. Handle the 3 ties with a single check first: <(you) = (friend)>. Of the 6 games left, exactly 3 are wins for you. What does "everything else" mean after that?

Show solution

One clear way is to start with a default answer, then let each winning combination overwrite it:

This is safe only because the four conditions never overlap: no single game is both a tie and a win. (Exercise 3 showed what happens when they do.)

With just 9 possible games, you can test every one of them. Here are the same rules in a text language, checked against all 9:

Across the 9 games there are 3 ties, 3 wins for you, and 3 wins for your friend, which is what a fair game should have.

#Exercise 5: Password length edge cases

A website says: passwords must be 8 to 12 characters long. The (length of (answer)) block in Operators reports how many characters were typed.

  1. Write the condition that is true for a valid length.
  2. List at least six test passwords with the result you expect, aimed at the edges.
Need a hint?

"8 to 12" includes both 8 and 12. A range check is two comparisons joined with and. For the tests, think: just below, on, and just above each end, plus one strange input.

Show solution
Test password Length Expected Why
sunfish 7 rejected one below the bottom edge
sunfish1 8 accepted exactly on the bottom edge
sunfish1234 11 accepted comfortably inside
sunfish12345 12 accepted exactly on the top edge
sunfish123456 13 rejected one above the top edge
(blank) 0 rejected nothing typed at all
eight spaces 8 accepted?! follows the rule, but is it a good password?

The last row is the kind of edge case that reveals a missing rule. The script does what the sign says, and the sign is probably wrong. That's a question for whoever owns the website.

#Exercise 6: Leap years

Here are the real rules for leap years:

  • A year divisible by 4 is a leap year,
  • except a year divisible by 100 is not,
  • except a year divisible by 400 is.

In Scratch, <((year) mod (4)) = (0)> is true when year divides evenly by 4. (mod gives the remainder after dividing, and a remainder of 0 means it divides evenly.) Build a script that asks for a year and says whether it's a leap year. Test 2024, 2023, 1900, 2000, and 2100.

Need a hint?

The rules are written from general to specific, but the script works best the other way round. Check the 400 rule first, then the 100 rule, then the 4 rule. Once a rule matches, you have your answer, so the rest belong in the else.

Show solution

If you checked the 4 rule first, 1900 would be called a leap year, because 1900 divides evenly by 4 and the script would never reach the exceptions. Here is the same decision in a text language, run on all five test years (% is Python's way of writing mod):

1900 and 2100 are the edge cases that trip most people up: divisible by 4 but not leap years.

#Challenge: Kiosk 2.0

Add two new rules to the library kiosk you built:

  1. Readers under 13 may have at most 3 books out. Everyone else may have 5.
  2. During July (the summer reading program), fines don't stop anyone from borrowing.

(current [month v]) in Sensing reports the month as a number from 1 to 12. Write your test table first: at least 10 rows, covering the edges of both new rules (ages 12 and 13, 2 and 3 books, June, July, and August).

Need a hint?

You can't wait until July to test the July rule. Make a month variable, set it from (current [month v]), and temporarily replace that with an ask while you're testing. Next module calls this a test mode.

Show solution

One way: ask for the age first and set [limit v] to 3 or 5 with an if/else. Change the books check to <(books out) > ((limit) - (1))>. Then wrap the fines check in if <not <(month) = (7)>> then … end, so it only runs outside July. Your table should include a 12-year-old with 3 books (refused), a 13-year-old with 3 books (allowed), and someone owing $20 in July (allowed) and in August (refused).

#A picture of "most specific first"

When rules have exceptions, and the exceptions have exceptions, draw them as a tree before you build. The leap-year rules look like this, with the most specific rule at the top:

The same shape works for the kiosk challenge, ticket prices with discounts, or any rule that comes with an "except when…".

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Describe a bug as a gap between expected and actual results.
  • Trace a script by hand with a table of variable values.
  • Recognize sequence bugs, condition bugs, and loop bugs.
  • Choose tests that break things on purpose, and make inputs controllable.
  • Follow a debugging routine that changes one thing at a time.

Sam built an alarm clock in Scratch. It worked perfectly on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday: 6:30 a.m., beep beep, time for school. On Friday it stayed silent and Sam was late. On Sunday it went off at 6:30 and woke up the whole house.

Here is Sam's script:

It looks fine. Monday through Friday are days 1 to 5, Saturday and Sunday are 6 and 7, so 6 or 7 means weekend. Except that Scratch doesn't count that way. The current [day of week] block reports 1 for Sunday and 7 for Saturday. Sam's script treated Friday (6) as a weekend and Sunday (1) as a school day.

Nothing crashed, no error appeared, and the script was right five days out of seven. That's typical: most bugs are small, quiet mismatches between what you think a block does and what it actually does.

#A bug is a gap between expected and actual

A bug is any difference between what a program should do (the expected result) and what it really does (the actual result). Here's Sam's week laid out that way:

Day day Expected Actual Match?
Monday 2 alarm alarm yes
Tuesday 3 alarm alarm yes
Wednesday 4 alarm alarm yes
Thursday 5 alarm alarm yes
Friday 6 alarm sleep in no
Saturday 7 sleep in sleep in yes
Sunday 1 sleep in alarm no

The table makes the bug impossible to miss, and the day column points straight at the cause. But it only works if the Expected column is written before you look at the Actual one. Run the program first, and it's easy to watch what it does and think "yep, looks right." So always predict first: before you click the green flag, write down what should happen.

#Trace it by hand: be the computer

Tracing means running a script in your head, one block at a time, writing down every variable as it changes. It's how you find bugs in code that runs too fast to watch.

Here's a countdown script to trace:

Step Block count Sprite says
1 set count to 3 3
2 check: is count 0? no 3
3 say count 3 3
4 change count by -1 2
5 check: is count 0? no 2
… … … …
11 check: is count 0? yes, leave loop 0
12 say Wake up! 0 Wake up!

It says 3, 2, 1, Wake up! That one's correct. Now predict: what happens if you change -1 to -2? Trace it before you read on.

The count goes 3, 1, -1, -3, and so on. It jumps right over 0, so count = 0 is never true and the loop never stops. A trace finds that in thirty seconds.

A computer can trace for you too. Here is Sam's alarm logic in a text language, Python, running through a whole week. for day in range(1, 8) means "for each day number from 1 to 7," and names turns a number into a day's name. Keep your eye on day and weekend:

#Three places bugs hide

Almost every logic bug lives in one of three places.

1. Sequence: the right blocks in the wrong order. This coin script shows the score before adding the points, so the player always sees the old score:

Swap the two blocks and it's fixed. A classic version of this bug is a set block that ended up inside a loop, so the variable gets reset on every pass.

2. Conditions: the wrong question. Sam's bug lives here. So does using > where you needed <, using or where the rule says and, or a boundary that's one off (> 5 when the rule means 5 or more). Condition bugs tend to show up only for certain inputs, which is why they survive so long.

3. Loops: the wrong number of repeats. A loop can run one time too many, one time too few, never stop, or never start. The countdown with -2 never stops. A safer stopping condition is repeat until <(count) < (1)>, which still works if the count skips past zero. Running one time too many or too few is so common it has a name: an off-by-one error.

#Test like you're trying to break it

Testing isn't about proving your program works. It's about finding the input that makes it fail before someone else does. Good tests come from four places:

  • Normal cases: a regular Wednesday.
  • Boundaries: the first and last school days of the week (Monday, Friday), and the days just past them.
  • Weird inputs: a holiday that falls on a weekday, a blank answer, a negative number.
  • Everything, when there are only a few possible inputs. A week has 7 days, so test all 7. Sam tested only Monday and would never have found the bug that way.

There's one more problem. Sam can't wait until Sunday to test Sunday. The fix is to make the input controllable: while testing, replace (current [day of week v]) with a value you choose, such as set [day v] to (1) or an ask block. Programmers call this a test mode. Once every test passes, you switch back to the real clock.

#A debugging routine that works

When a test fails, guessing and changing random blocks usually makes things worse. Follow the same routine every time:

Scratch gives you good tools for the "find the first block" step:

  • Click a block to run it alone. Click a reporter like (current [day of week v]) and a bubble shows its value right now. That alone would have caught Sam's bug.
  • Show variable monitors. Tick the checkbox next to a variable in the Variables category to watch it change on the stage.
  • Add a temporary say. Drop say (day) for (1) seconds into the middle of a script to see a value at that exact moment.
  • Slow it down. A wait (1) seconds inside a fast loop lets your eyes keep up.
  • Click Debug. The Scratch editor's top bar has a Debug button that opens a list of tips for getting unstuck.

When you're truly stuck, explain the script out loud, block by block, to a friend or to anything that will sit still. Programmers call this rubber duck debugging, because some keep a real rubber duck on the desk for it. Saying "and then this block sets day to..." is often when you hear the mistake.

⚠️ Watch out

Changing several things at once. If you change three blocks and the bug disappears, you don't know which change fixed it, or whether the other two broke something new. Change one thing, re-run the tests, then decide on the next change.

⚠️ Watch out

Re-running only the test that failed. Sam fixes Sunday by changing 6 to 1, checks Sunday, and stops. But a fix can break a different case, or uncover a bug that the first one was hiding. Re-run the whole test table after every change.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A countdown starts at count = 10, runs repeat until <(count) = (0)>, and does change [count v] by (-3) each pass. What happens?

  • After 1 comes -2, and the loop only stops at exactly 0.

  • 10, 7, 4, 1, -2, -5… never lands exactly on 0, so the stopping condition is never true.

  • Subtracting 3 from 10 never gives exactly 0.

Show answer

B. 10, 7, 4, 1, -2, -5… never lands exactly on 0, so the stopping condition is never true.

2Sam fixes his weekend check to <<(day) = (1)> or <(day) = (7)>>. Which tests should he run now?

  • A fix can break other days. Friday was broken too, and he wouldn't know if it's fixed.

  • Better, but the fix could have broken Saturday or a weekday. Seven tests are cheap.

  • There are only 7 possible inputs, so testing all of them proves the whole week is right.

Show answer

C. There are only 7 possible inputs, so testing all of them proves the whole week is right.

3In a game, the score display always shows 10 points less than the real score. What kind of bug is most likely?

  • The display is always exactly one coin behind, which points to the order of the blocks.

  • Too many repeats would give a score that's too high, not one that lags by one coin.

  • There's no decision involved in showing a score, so a comparison is unlikely to be the cause.

Show answer

A. The display is always exactly one coin behind, which points to the order of the blocks.

Key takeaways

  • A bug is a gap between expected and actual. Write the expected result first.
  • Tracing a script by hand, with a table of values, finds bugs that run too fast to see.
  • Bugs hide in sequence (wrong order), conditions (wrong question), and loops (wrong number of repeats).
  • Test normal cases, boundaries, weird inputs, and every input when there are only a few.
  • Make inputs controllable with a test mode, change one thing at a time, and re-run every test after every fix.

#Further reading

  • Debugging Scripts (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): Scratch-specific tips, including the most common causes of broken scripts.
  • Off-by-one error (Wikipedia) (opens in a new tab): the bug that's so common it got a name, with the famous fence-post puzzle.
  • Rubber duck debugging (Wikipedia) (opens in a new tab): where the idea came from and why explaining code out loud works.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Add a test mode so you can choose the day and date instead of waiting for them.
  • Write a test plan, with expected results, before running anything.
  • Find and fix a condition bug, a sequence bug, and a loop bug, one at a time.
  • Re-run the whole test plan after every fix, and notice when a fix uncovers a new bug.

#What we're building

Sam's alarm is getting an upgrade. The new version should:

  • ring at 6:30 a.m. on school days (Monday to Friday),
  • stay quiet on Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays,
  • ring exactly 3 times, then stop.

Sam already wrote it, and it's wrong in three different ways. You'll build Sam's version exactly as written, test it properly, and fix it. When you're done, it will pass this plan:

The alarm's logic has two questions in a row and one loop:

#Step 1: Make the variables and the holiday list

  1. Open scratch.mit.edu (opens in a new tab), click Create, and keep the cat as your alarm clock.
  2. In Variables, click Make a Variable and create day, today, alarm, and rings.
  3. Click Make a List and create a list called holidays. An empty list box appears on the stage.
  4. Build this small stack of list blocks (no hat block on top) and click it once:

The list box on the stage fills with three dates. Lists are saved with the project, so you only need to click the stack once (and again if you ever change it). The dates are stored as month/day text, like 12/25, so the holiday check can compare them directly.

#Step 2: Build Sam's script, with a test mode

Sam's real version reads the day from (current [day of week v]). You can't wait for Sunday to test Sunday, so this version asks for the day and date instead. That's the test mode, and you'll switch it off at the end.

The contains block is in Variables, below the list blocks. Build the script exactly like this, bugs and all: fixing things before you've seen them fail teaches you nothing about finding them.

#Step 3: Write the test plan first, then run it

Here's the plan. The Expected column comes from the requirements, written before anyone clicked the green flag. Copy it onto paper with the Actual column blank.

# Test day today Expected Actual
1 Monday 2 3/9 3 rings
2 Friday 6 3/13 3 rings
3 Saturday 7 3/14 sleep in
4 Sunday 1 3/15 sleep in
5 Holiday, Friday 6 12/25 sleep in
6 Holiday, Saturday 7 7/4 sleep in

Run each test in Scratch. Tick the checkbox next to rings so you can see it on the stage, and count the BEEPs.

Here is Sam's logic in a text language, Python, running the same plan. Each if and else matches a block in the script, and while not rings > 3 is Python's way of saying repeat until <(rings) > (3)>. Your Scratch results should match its output:

Three failures out of six, and that's good news: you now have exact evidence. There are two different symptoms. Friday and Sunday get the wrong decision, and the days that ring get 4 rings instead of 3. Fix one bug at a time, starting with the decision.

#Step 4: Fix bug 1, the day numbers

The Friday and Sunday failures point at the weekend check. Is 6 really Saturday? Find out with evidence, not memory: in the Sensing category, click the (current [day of week v]) block itself. A bubble pops up with today's number. Compare it with today's actual day, and you'll find that Scratch counts 1 = Sunday up to 7 = Saturday.

So Sam's 6 or 7 meant Friday or Saturday. Change the 6 to 1:

Now re-run the whole plan, not just the two failed tests:

Sunday passes now, and Friday rings (4 times, but that's the loop bug, which comes later). Now look at test 5: the Christmas test passed before and fails now. Bug 1 was hiding a second bug. The wrong day numbers happened to treat Friday 12/25 as a weekend, which covered up a broken holiday check. Re-running only the Sunday test would never have shown it.

#Step 5: Fix bug 2, the order of the checks

Trace test 5 by hand and write down alarm after each block:

Block alarm
set alarm to on on
holiday check: 12/25 is in the list, so set alarm to off off
weekend check: day 6 isn't 1 or 7, so the else runs set alarm to on on

There it is. The holiday check works, and then the weekend check's else overwrites it a moment later. This is a sequence bug: each block does its own job correctly, but the second one undoes the first.

You can see it happen in Scratch, too. Add a temporary say (alarm) for (1) seconds just after each of the two if blocks and run test 5. You'll see off, then on.

The cleanest fix is to ask one combined question, so nothing can overwrite anything. Delete both if blocks and the set [alarm v] to [on] above them, and put this in their place:

Read it out loud: "if it's a holiday, or it's Sunday, or it's Saturday, the alarm is off. Otherwise it's on." Run all six tests again. Test 5 passes, and only the ring-count failures are left.

#Step 6: Fix bug 3, the extra ring

Every school day rings 4 times. Watch the rings monitor during a test: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Here is the loop on its own, as a text-language trace, so you can watch exactly when it decides to stop:

The loop checks rings > 3 before each ring. At 0, 1, 2, and 3 the answer is no, so it rings four times, and only stops at 4. That's an off-by-one error: the stopping condition is one step too late.

You could change it to repeat until <(rings) = (3)>, but Scratch has a block that says exactly what the requirement says. Replace the whole repeat until loop with:

The rings counter isn't needed any more, so you can delete the set [rings v] to (0) block too. The wait (0.5) seconds adds a gap between the bubbles so you can count three separate rings.

#Step 7: Re-run everything, then switch off test mode

One last full run of the plan, with all three fixes:

Six out of six. Run the six tests in Scratch too, and check every row of your Actual column matches.

Now switch test mode off. Replace the two ask blocks and their set blocks with the real clock, and add a wait until so the alarm really waits for 6:30. Scratch's current [hour] uses 24-hour time, so 6:30 a.m. is hour 6, minute 30.

Moving to the real clock raises two new edge cases, so think them through before you build:

  • When is the day checked? If the script reads the day once, when you click the green flag, then starting it on Sunday evening means it decides "Sleep in!" and never rings on Monday. The day has to be read each morning at 6:30, inside a forever loop.
  • What happens after the rings? Three rings take about 5 seconds. Then the loop goes back to wait until 6:30, and it's still 6:30, so it would ring again and again for the whole minute. A second wait until makes it wait for the minute to change first.

#The finished alarm

The join blocks build today's date as text in the same month/day shape as the list, like 3/9, so contains can match it. The alarm variable has gone: once the decision was a single if/else, it had nothing left to remember. To try the real-clock version without waking up at 6:30, temporarily change the hour and minute in the wait until to a time two minutes from now.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why did the Christmas test pass with Sam's original script but fail after the first fix?

  • The list never changed. The holiday check was already broken.

  • Two bugs cancelled each other out for that one test. Fixing one revealed the other, and only re-running the whole plan showed it.

  • 12/25 is in the list, and the trace in Step 5 shows the holiday check working.

Show answer

B. Two bugs cancelled each other out for that one test. Fixing one revealed the other, and only re-running the whole plan showed it.

2Why does the build use ask blocks for the day and date instead of the real clock while testing?

  • current [day of week] works fine. It just always gives today's answer.

  • A test mode makes the input controllable, so every row of the plan can be run in a few minutes.

  • Speed isn't the reason. Control over the input is.

Show answer

B. A test mode makes the input controllable, so every row of the plan can be run in a few minutes.

3The original loop was repeat until <(rings) > (3)> with rings starting at 0. Why did it ring 4 times?

  • say runs once each time the loop body runs.

  • It started at 0, which is part of why there was one extra ring.

  • The loop only stops once rings reaches 4: a classic off-by-one error.

Show answer

C. The loop only stops once rings reaches 4: a classic off-by-one error.

Key takeaways

  • Build the buggy version as written, then let a test plan show you exactly what's wrong.
  • Use evidence: click a reporter block to see its real value instead of trusting your memory.
  • One bug can hide another. Re-run the whole plan after every fix, not just the failing test.
  • If one check overwrites another, combine them into a single decision.
  • When the requirement says "exactly 3 times," repeat (3) says it directly and leaves no room for off-by-one errors.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Summer break: no alarm in July or August. Add at least four tests: June 30, July 1, August 31, and September 1.
  • Snooze: pressing the space bar during the BEEPs snoozes for 5 minutes. Test pressing it twice.
  • Holiday editor: let someone type a new holiday into the list. What should happen if it's already there?

#Further reading

  • Current () (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): every option of the clock block, including the Sunday-is-1 day numbering.
  • List (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): how lists work in Scratch, with all the list blocks in one place.
  • Debugging Help (Scratch Wiki) (opens in a new tab): what each tip behind the editor's Debug button means.

m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Predict a script's output by tracing it with a table of values.
  • Pick test inputs that make a hidden bug show itself.
  • Name each bug as a sequence, condition, or loop bug, and fix it.
  • Re-test with a plan instead of trying one input and hoping.

Every script below has something wrong with it, except the warm-up. For each one: predict first, trace if you need to, find the bug, fix it, then test the fix with more than one input. Build the scripts in Scratch if you want to see them fail for real.

#Warm-up: what does it say?

Predict the final value before you build it.

Show solution

It says 16. change [x v] by (x) adds x to itself, which doubles it: 2 → 4 → 8 → 16. Three passes, three doublings. If you guessed 8, you probably counted the starting value as a pass.

#Exercise 1: Fill in the trace table

Trace this script on paper. Make a table with columns for the step, n, and total, and fill in a row every time a variable changes. What does the sprite say?

Need a hint?

The loop checks n > 4 at the top of every pass. The body runs while that's false, so it runs with n = 1, 2, 3, and 4. What is total after each one?

Show solution
After n total
the two set blocks 1 0
pass 1 2 1
pass 2 3 3
pass 3 4 6
pass 4 5 10

At the next check, 5 > 4 is true, so the loop ends and the sprite says 10 (1 + 2 + 3 + 4). Here is the same loop in a text language, printing a row each pass so you can check your table:

#Exercise 2: The invisible square

This script should draw a square with the Pen extension (click Add Extension at the bottom left of the editor, then choose Pen). It runs without any error, but nothing appears on the stage. Find the bug and fix it.

Need a hint?

Every block here is the right block. Is each one in the right place? Read the script aloud as instructions to a person holding a pen.

Show solution

It's a sequence bug: pen down comes after the drawing, so the sprite walks the whole square with the pen up, then puts the pen down at the very end. Move pen down up to just before repeat (4):

The extra pen up blocks at the start and end are good habits: the sprite won't leave a stray line when it jumps to the start, or when the project runs again.

#Exercise 3: Counting to 10, almost

This should say every number from 1 to 10. Before you build it, predict the last number it says. Then fix it in two different ways.

Need a hint?

Trace just the last two passes. When n becomes 10, what happens at the top of the loop before anything is said?

Show solution

It says 1 to 9. When n reaches 10, the loop's check is true, so it stops before saying 10. That's an off-by-one loop bug.

Fix 1: change the condition to repeat until <(n) > (10)>, so the body still runs when n is 10.

Fix 2: say exactly what you mean with a counting loop:

For both fixes, test the first and last numbers said, not just "it counts."

#Exercise 4: Which version is broken?

A shop promises free shipping on orders of $50 or more. Three programmers wrote the check three ways:

Each one says "Free shipping!" when its condition is true. Choose three test totals that, between them, prove which versions are wrong. Then fill in a table of expected and actual results for all three versions.

Need a hint?

Each wrong version fails at a different total. One is wrong exactly on the boundary. The other is wrong for an amount with cents, just under the boundary.

Show solution

Use $49.50, $50.00, and $60.00.

Total Expected A: > 50 B: not < 50 C: > 49
$49.50 no no no yes (wrong)
$50.00 yes no (wrong) yes yes
$60.00 yes yes yes yes

Version A fails on the boundary. Version C only fails with cents, so if you'd tested whole-dollar totals like $49 and $50, it would have looked perfect. Version B is the correct one. Notice that $60 doesn't catch anything: tests far from the boundary rarely do.

#Exercise 5: The sprite that won't stop

The sprite should glide right and stop at x = 200. Instead it slides to the right edge of the stage and stays pressed against it. The script never ends. Why?

Need a hint?

Write down the x positions the sprite visits: 0, 15, 30… Does 200 ever appear in that list?

Show solution

x goes 0, 15, 30, …, 180, 195, 210. It jumps straight over 200, so x position = 200 is never true and the loop runs forever. This is a loop bug caused by an exact-match stopping condition. Stop on "reached or passed" instead:

Exact = checks are fine for stopping a loop only when you're certain the value lands on that number. With steps of 15, it never lands on 200. Test your fix with a different step size too, like 7 or 40.

#Exercise 6: The warmest day of the week

A list called temps holds seven daily temperatures. This script should say the highest one. Find two bugs. For each, write a test list that exposes it.

Need a hint?

For the first bug: which item does the if look at on the second pass? On the third? For the second bug, think about a very cold week in Minnesota or northern Canada.

Show solution

Bug 1 (loop): i never changes, so every pass looks at item 1 again. The test list 3, 9, 4 exposes it: the script says 3 instead of 9. Fix it by adding change [i v] by (1) at the end of the loop body.

Bug 2 (edge case): warmest starts at 0. In a week where every day is below freezing, like -5, -12, -3, nothing is bigger than 0, so the script says 0, a temperature that never happened. Fix it by starting with the first item instead: set [warmest v] to (item (1) of [temps v]).

Here is the fixed version in a text language, run against a whole test plan at once. Notice the tests that put the biggest value first, last, and in the middle:

#Challenge: Three bugs, one of each kind

This quiz should ask "What is 1 + 5?", then "2 + 5?", then "3 + 5?", and report how many you got right out of 3. It has exactly one sequence bug, one condition bug, and one loop bug. Write a test plan first (what do you type, and what score do you expect?), then find and fix all three.

Need a hint?

Good tests: answer all three correctly (expect 3), answer all three wrong (expect 0), and get only the first one right (expect 1). Watch the score and question monitors while you run each test.

Show solution
  • Sequence bug: set [score v] to (0) is inside the loop, so the score resets before every question and can never be more than 1. Delete the copy inside the loop.
  • Condition bug: the correct answer is (question) + (5), not + (6). Typing 6 for "1 + 5" is marked wrong.
  • Loop bug: question never changes, so the quiz asks "What is 1 + 5?" three times. Add change [question v] by (1) at the end of the loop body.

With all three fixes, the three test runs should report scores of 3, 0, and 1.

#Which kind of bug is it?

When a test fails, the pattern of the failure is a strong clue about where to look:

It's a starting point, not a rule. The invisible square was wrong every single time (order). The shipping checks were right everywhere except near $50 (conditions). The sprite that wouldn't stop never finished at all (loop).

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why two correct algorithms can still be very different.
  • Run linear search and binary search by hand, and count their checks.
  • Describe the best case and worst case of an algorithm.
  • Predict how step counts grow when the input gets bigger.
  • Sort a small list with selection sort and count its comparisons.

I'm thinking of a whole number from 1 to 100. You guess, and I tell you "higher" or "lower." How many guesses do you need?

If you guess 1, then 2, then 3, and so on, you'll always find it eventually. But if my number is 100, that's 100 guesses. There's another way that never needs more than 7, whatever the number is. And for a number from 1 to a million, that second way never needs more than 20.

Both ways are correct. They both always find the number. But one of them is wildly faster, and that difference is what this module is about: how to compare algorithms that all work, and pick the best one for the job.

#Two right answers can still be different

When two teams solve the same problem in different ways, "does it work?" is only the first question. The next ones are:

  • How many steps does it take? Not seconds, because a fast laptop and an old tablet would give different times for the same algorithm. Count the main action instead: guesses, checks, comparisons, swaps.
  • What's the best case and the worst case? In the counting-up game, the best case is my number being 1 (one guess). The worst case is 100 (a hundred guesses). The worst case is usually the one that matters, because it's the promise you can make.
  • What does it need? Some algorithms only work if the data is already sorted, or if there's enough space.
  • Is it clear? A slightly slower algorithm that everyone understands can beat a fast one nobody can check.

#Linear search: check every item in order

Linear search is the counting-up strategy. Here it is in plain English:

  1. Look at the first item.
  2. If it's the one you want, stop: you found it.
  3. Otherwise, move to the next item and go back to step 2.
  4. If you run out of items, it isn't there.

This is how you look for your phone in a lost-and-found box: pick things up one at a time. In Scratch, with a list called box and a variable target:

And here it is in a text language, Python, counting each check as it goes. for item in box means "take each item from the box in turn," and break means "stop the loop right now," like Scratch's stop block. Step through it and watch checks:

Five checks for the phone. The best case is 1 check (it's on top). The worst case is 6: the phone is at the bottom, or it isn't there at all, and you can only know that by checking everything. For a box of n items, linear search needs up to n checks.

The upside: linear search works on any list, in any order. The box doesn't need to be organized.

#Binary search: throw away half every time

The 7-guess strategy for the number game is binary search. Guess the middle (50). If I say "higher," every number from 1 to 50 is gone in one guess. Guess the middle of what's left (75), and half of that is gone. Each guess cuts the problem in half.

This only works because the numbers are in order. "Higher" tells you something about all the numbers below your guess. In a jumbled list, the middle item tells you nothing about the others.

The plain-English steps, for a sorted list:

  1. Look at the middle item of the part you haven't ruled out.
  2. If it's the target, stop.
  3. If the target comes before it, rule out the middle and everything after it. Otherwise rule out the middle and everything before it.
  4. If nothing is left, the target isn't there. Otherwise go back to step 1.

Here it is in Python on 15 sorted locker numbers. Two details: Python counts positions from 0, so the first locker is position 0 and the last is position 14. And // means "divide and round down," which finds the middle position. Keep your eye on low and high, the two ends of the part that's still in play:

Four checks: 34, 58, 70, 63. With 15 lockers, that's the worst case. Linear search could have needed 15.

#How the step counts grow

The real difference shows up as lists get bigger. Here is the worst case for both searches. The binary_worst function counts how many times you can halve a list before nothing is left, which is the most checks binary search can ever need:

The last row is roughly every person on Earth. If everyone's name were in one sorted list, binary search would find anyone in at most 33 checks.

Notice the pattern. When the list gets 10 times bigger, linear search needs 10 times as many checks. Binary search needs only about 3 more. Doubling the list adds just one binary check, because the first check cuts it back down to the old size. Here's what that looks like on a chart:

#Sorting: the price of binary search

Binary search needs sorted data, and sorting takes steps too. One of the simplest sorting algorithms is selection sort. You can do it with five playing cards right now:

  1. Look through all the cards and find the smallest.
  2. Swap it into the first position.
  3. Now ignore the first card and repeat with the rest: find the smallest, swap it into the second position.
  4. Keep going until only one card is left.

Here it is in Python with a counter for comparisons (each time two cards are compared). The line cards[start], cards[smallest] = cards[smallest], cards[start] swaps two cards' places:

Five cards take 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons. For 100 cards it's 99 + 98 + … + 1 = 4,950. Sorting is much more expensive than a single search.

So which should you use? It depends on how often you search:

  • Search once, in a jumble: linear search. Sorting first would cost far more than it saves.
  • Search many times: sort once, then use binary search every time. That's why dictionaries, phone contact lists, and library catalogs are kept in order. The sorting cost is paid once, and every lookup after that is fast.

⚠️ Watch out

Binary search on a list that isn't sorted. It doesn't crash. It just gives wrong answers:

Both lists contain 1. In the jumbled one, the middle is 9, so the search throws away the right half, then sees 8 and throws away everything else, and reports "not found." Always check the input is sorted first.

⚠️ Watch out

Judging an algorithm by one lucky run. If you test the counting-up strategy with the secret number 3, it looks brilliant: 3 guesses! Compare algorithms on their worst case, or on the average over many inputs, never on a single run.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You play the guessing game with numbers from 1 to 1,000, always guessing the middle. What's the most guesses you'll ever need?

  • That's about what linear search needs on average. Halving is much faster.

  • Each wrong guess roughly halves what's left: 1,000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 62 → 31 → 15 → 7 → 3 → 1. That's ten sizes, so at most ten guesses.

  • That's the worst case for counting up, not for halving.

Show answer

B. Each wrong guess roughly halves what's left: 1,000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 62 → 31 → 15 → 7 → 3 → 1. That's ten sizes, so at most ten guesses.

2A sorted list grows from 500 names to 1,000 names. What happens to the worst-case checks?

  • That's true for linear search only.

  • Binary search's first check cuts 1,000 back to 500, so doubling the list adds just one step.

  • Linear search has to check every name, so more names means more checks.

Show answer

B. Binary search's first check cuts 1,000 back to 500, so doubling the list adds just one step.

3You're looking for your friend's jacket in a heap of 30 coats, just once. Which approach makes sense?

  • The heap isn't sorted, and sorting 30 coats to search once would take far more steps than just looking.

  • Sorting costs far more than one search saves. It only pays off if you'll search many times.

  • The heap isn't in order, so the middle coat tells you nothing about the others.

Show answer

A. The heap isn't sorted, and sorting 30 coats to search once would take far more steps than just looking.

4How many comparisons does selection sort make on 6 cards?

  • Each pass compares the current card with all the cards after it, so it's more than one per card.

  • That would be comparing every card with every card, including itself.

  • 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. Each pass has one fewer card left to look through.

Show answer

C. 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. Each pass has one fewer card left to look through.

Key takeaways

  • Two correct algorithms can need very different numbers of steps. Compare them by counting the main action, not by timing them.
  • Linear search works on any list and needs up to n checks for n items.
  • Binary search needs a sorted list and halves the problem each check: at most 10 checks for 1,000 items, and 20 for a million.
  • Selection sort on n cards makes (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 comparisons. Sorting is worth it when you'll search many times.
  • Judge an algorithm by its worst case (or average), never by one lucky run.
